Why: "Which" already stands for the book, so the pronoun "it" repeats the object and is not needed.
Our class is quite different with the other sections. Is "with" right?

Our class is quite different from the other sections.
Why: "Different" is usually followed by "from". Some British speakers also say "different to".
On Diwali we light diyas, and eats sweets with our relatives. Please correct.

On Diwali we light diyas and eat sweets with our relatives.
Why: The verb must match "we", so it is "eat". Also, no comma is needed before "and" when both verbs share one subject.
It rains a lot in July, but today is not raining. Fix this.

It rains a lot in July, but today it is not raining.
Why: English weather verbs need "it" as the subject, and "today" cannot play that role.
The market closes at nine, so we should leave soon. Is the tense okay?

Your tense is fine.
Why: The simple present "closes" is the normal tense for a regular timetable.
Is there any hotels near the bus stand? Please correct.

Are there any hotels near the bus stand?
Why: "Hotels" is plural, so the question begins with "are there".
My grandmother is knowing many old stories. Please correct.

My grandmother knows many old stories.
Why: "Know" describes a state, and state verbs are not usually used in the continuous form.
Please give me a glass of water, I am very thirsty Check my punctuation.

Please give me a glass of water. I am very thirsty.
Why: Two complete sentences should not be joined with only a comma, and the last sentence needs a full stop.
My phone battery gets drained very fastly. Is "fastly" a word?

My phone battery gets drained very fast.
Why: "Fast" is both an adjective and an adverb, and "fastly" is not used in standard English.
He is working in this company for three years. Fix the tense please.

He has been working in this company for three years.
Why: "For three years" describes a period that continues up to now, so use the present perfect continuous.
Both of my friends is coming to my birthday party. Correct this.

Both of my friends are coming to my birthday party.
Why: "Both" means two, so the verb is plural: "are".
The injured bird couldn't flew away. What should the verb be?

The injured bird couldn't fly away.
Why: After "couldn't" (a modal verb), use the base form "fly", not the past "flew".
I was born in a city which name is Nashik. Fix the relative word.

I was born in a city whose name is Nashik.
Why: "Whose" shows that the name belongs to the city. "Which name" does not work as a relative phrase.
I didn't buy nothing at the shop today. Please fix.

I didn't buy anything at the shop today.
Why: "Didn't" already makes the sentence negative, so use "anything" instead of a second negative, "nothing".
The exam will start from nine o'clock. Can you check the preposition?

The exam will start at nine o'clock.
Why: Use "at" for a clock time.
I felt very nervous before my speech, but it went good. Fix please.

I felt very nervous before my speech, but it went well.
Why: "Went" is a verb, so it takes the adverb "well", not the adjective "good".
She plays the guitar very good and sings beautiful. Tell me what is wrong.

She plays the guitar very well and sings beautifully.
Why: Words that describe how a verb is done must be adverbs: "well" and "beautifully".
If it rains tomorrow, we will stay at home. Is the verb pattern right?

Yes, that is right.
Why: This is the usual pattern for a real future possibility: present tense in the "if" part and "will" in the main part.
I like to collecting old stamps. Please correct me.

I like to collect old stamps.
Why: After "to" use the base verb. You can also say "I like collecting old stamps", without "to".
A old man lives next to us, and he is very friendly. Is "A old" fine?

An old man lives next to us, and he is very friendly.
Why: Use "an" before a word that begins with a vowel sound, such as "old".
We got down from the bus at the wrong stop. Is "got down" okay?

We got off the bus at the wrong stop.
Why: "Get off" is the usual international phrase for leaving a bus. "Got down from the bus" is common in Indian English, but readers elsewhere may not expect it.
The kids was playing hide and seek when I came. Please check.

The kids were playing hide and seek when I came.
Why: "Kids" is plural, so the past form is "were".
Scientists have discovered a new species of frogs in the forests. Is "species" right here?

That sentence is right.
Why: "Species" has the same form in singular and plural, so "a new species" is correct, and "of frogs" is fine.
She can speaks four languages fluently. What should it be?

She can speak four languages fluently.
Why: After a modal verb such as "can", the main verb stays in its base form.
I wake up at six and then I am brushing my teeth every morning. Fix this.

I wake up at six and then I brush my teeth every morning.
Why: A daily habit uses the simple present, not the present continuous.
My mother cooks very tasty food than my aunt. Please repair it.

My mother cooks tastier food than my aunt.
Why: "Than" needs a comparative form, "tastier", and "very" cannot be used with a comparative.
Their's house is at the end of the lane. Is that spelled right?

Their house is at the end of the lane.
Why: Before a noun, use "their". "Theirs" stands alone, and it never has an apostrophe.
The vendor gave me discount because I bought two shirts. Fix?

The vendor gave me a discount because I bought two shirts.
Why: Here "discount" names one reduction in price, which usually takes "a". Some speakers drop the article in casual talk.
Yesterday was more hot than today, isn't it? Please correct both parts.

Yesterday was hotter than today, wasn't it?
Why: Short adjectives like "hot" take -er for the comparative. The tag question repeats the verb and tense of the statement: "was", so "wasn't".
The function will be started at six, so please come in time. Can you improve it?

The function will start at six, so please come on time.
Why: "Start" is usually active here, since the function begins by itself. "On time" means punctually, while "in time" means early enough.
We went on a trip by our own car. Is "by" okay?

We went on a trip in our own car.
Why: "By car" is the fixed phrase without a possessive, but with "our own" we say "in".
He suggested me to take a day off. Please fix it.

He suggested that I take a day off.
Why: "Suggest" is not followed by a person and "to". Use a "that" clause, or say "suggested taking a day off".
Kerala is located in south of India. What is missing?

Kerala is located in the south of India.
Why: "South" is used as a noun here, so it needs "the".
She painted a beautiful picture of a peacock with a brush thin. Please check.

She painted a beautiful picture of a peacock with a thin brush.
Why: In English an adjective comes before the noun it describes.
First cut the onions in small pieces, than add them to hot oil. Two mistakes I think.

First cut the onions into small pieces, then add them to hot oil.
Why: "Cut into small pieces" is the more usual phrase for the pieces that result. "Then" shows the next step, while "than" is for comparisons.
The teacher asked us to submit the project until Friday. Is that okay?

The teacher asked us to submit the project by Friday.
Why: "By" gives a deadline. "Until" is for something that continues up to a time.
We seen a funny film last night. Can you correct it?

We saw a funny film last night.
Why: "Seen" needs a helper such as "have". With "last night" the simple past "saw" is used.
There are two metro station near my house. Correct please.

There are two metro stations near my house.
Why: After "two", the noun must be plural.
Our neighbours are very kind peoples. What is wrong?

Our neighbours are very kind people.
Why: "People" is already the plural of "person", so it takes no -s in this sense.
I will invite all my friends in my birthday. Fix the preposition.

I will invite all my friends to my birthday.
Why: We invite someone "to" an event, not "in" it.
During Holi, children throw coloured powder at each other. Is the preposition correct?

The preposition is fine.
Why: "Throw at" is the right pattern when something is thrown toward a person, and "each other" fits two or more people.
I recieved your invitation and I will definately come. Spelling mistakes?

I received your invitation and I will definitely come.
Why: "Received" follows the rule "i before e, except after c". "Definitely" is spelled with -ite- in the middle.

Whats the name of the book you're reading
Can you fix the punctuation?

What's the name of the book you're reading?
Why: The contraction of "what is" needs an apostrophe, and a direct question ends with a question mark.
My younger brother is very naughty, he break everything he touches. Please correct.

My younger brother is very naughty. He breaks everything he touches.
Why: The verb for "he" takes -s. Also, two full sentences should be separated by a full stop, not a comma.
Always I forget to bring my water bottle. How can I say it better?

I always forget to bring my water bottle.
Why: A frequency word such as "always" usually goes before the main verb.
Please make your homework before dinner. Is "make" okay?

Please do your homework before dinner.
Why: The usual phrase is "do homework". "Make" is used for creating something new.
We took taxi from airport to hotel. Please correct this.

We took a taxi from the airport to the hotel.
Why: A singular countable noun needs an article. "The" fits here because the airport and the hotel are specific places.
I bought three kilo of mangoes and two dozens of bananas. What should change?

I bought three kilos of mangoes and two dozen bananas.
Why: "Kilo" usually takes -s after a number, but "dozen" stays singular after a number and is not followed by "of" in this pattern.
He is the more tall player in our team. Can you correct it?

He is the tallest player in our team.
Why: Comparing one with the whole team needs the superlative. "Tall" is short, so it takes -est.
How much eggs do we need for the cake? Please fix.

How many eggs do we need for the cake?
Why: Use "many" with countable plural nouns such as "eggs".
There is few water in the well this summer. Is "few" right?

There is little water in the well this summer.
Why: "Water" is uncountable, so it takes "little". "Few" goes with countable plural nouns.
Each of the students have a library card. Which verb is right?

Each of the students has a library card.
Why: "Each" is singular, so formal English uses "has". You may hear "have" in casual speech.
She enjoys to paint landscapes on Sundays. Please correct.

She enjoys painting landscapes on Sundays.
Why: "Enjoy" is followed by the -ing form, not "to" plus a verb.
The report was wrote by the new interns. Fix the verb?

The report was written by the new interns.
Why: A passive sentence needs the past participle, "written", after "was".
He said me that he will come late. Two things sound wrong.

He told me that he would come late.
Why: "Say" does not take a person directly, but "tell" does. In reported speech "would" is the usual choice after a past verb, though "will" is possible if the plan is still ahead.
Excuse me, which is the way for the railway station? Please correct.

Excuse me, which is the way to the railway station?
Why: We say "the way to" a place.
My parents got married twenty years before. What is wrong?

My parents got married twenty years ago.
Why: "Ago" counts back from the present moment, so it fits here. "Before" needs another past point to count from.
I am too happy to see you again. Please fix the word.

I am so happy to see you again.
Why: "Too" suggests a problem, as in "too hot". For strong, good feeling, use "so" or "very".
The room is enough big for six people. Anything to change?

The room is big enough for six people.
Why: "Enough" comes after an adjective, but before a noun.
I spend most of my free time to read comics. Is "to read" okay?

I spend most of my free time reading comics.
Why: After "spend time", use the -ing form of the verb.
The girl who sits next to me is from Kerala. Is "who" right?

It is correct as written.
Why: "Who" is the correct relative pronoun for a person, and "sits" agrees with "who", which stands for one girl.
Their going to the cricket match, and they're tickets are in there bag. Can you sort out their/there/they're for me?

They're going to the cricket match, and their tickets are in their bag.
Why: "They're" means "they are", and "their" shows ownership. "There" is for place.
Your very good at singing, you're voice is lovely. Please correct.

You're very good at singing. Your voice is lovely.
Why: "You're" means "you are", while "your" shows ownership. Two full sentences should be separated by a full stop, not a comma.
I don't want to loose my chess match again. Spelling check please.

I don't want to lose my chess match again.
Why: "Lose" means to fail to win or keep. "Loose" means not tight.
Trees gives us shade and fresh air, so we should not cut down them. Two mistakes?

Trees give us shade and fresh air, so we should not cut them down.
Why: "Trees" is plural, so the verb is "give". With the phrasal verb "cut down", a pronoun object goes in the middle.
Please keep the spare keys in a safe place so that nobody can't find them. Fix please.

Please keep the spare keys in a safe place so that nobody can find them.
Why: "Nobody" is already negative, so a second negative with "can't" is not used in standard English.
Have you visited Jaipur last year? Please fix the tense.

Did you visit Jaipur last year?
Why: "Last year" is a finished time, so use the simple past with "did" rather than the present perfect.
I usually get up on six o'clock and go to school with bus. Fix please.

I usually get up at six o'clock and go to school by bus.
Why: Use "at" with a clock time, and "by" for the means of transport.
The children listened careful to the story. What is the problem?

The children listened carefully to the story.
Why: The word describes how they listened, so it must be an adverb, "carefully".
My parents they are working in the same school. What is extra?

My parents are working in the same school.
Why: "They" repeats the subject "my parents", so it is not needed.
There were less people at the temple today. Which is better, less or fewer?

There were fewer people at the temple today.
Why: In careful English, "fewer" goes with countable nouns such as "people". "Less" is often heard in speech.
The hero enters the room and picked up a letter. Something is off.

The hero enters the room and picks up a letter.
Why: When you retell a story in the present, keep both verbs in the same tense. You could also use the past for both.
Don't forget turning off the lights before going out. Please check.

Don't forget to turn off the lights before going out.
Why: "Forget to" plus a verb is used for something you need to remember to do.
I wish I can speak English more confidently. Fix it?

I wish I could speak English more confidently.
Why: After "wish" about a present situation that is not true, use the past form, "could".
My cousin told me a very funny joke, but I didn't understood it. Fix me.

My cousin told me a very funny joke, but I didn't understand it.
Why: After "didn't", the main verb takes its base form, "understand".
The womens hostel is next to the library. Where does the apostrophe go?

The women's hostel is next to the library.
Why: "Women" is an irregular plural that does not end in -s, so the possessive is "'s".
I have been in Goa two times. Fix the wording.

I have been to Goa twice.
Why: "Been to" is the usual phrase for visits, and "twice" is the natural word for two times.
My brother likes cricket and so I do. Is the word order okay?

My brother likes cricket, and so do I.
Why: After "so" meaning "also", the helper verb comes before the subject. A comma before "and" also helps here.
My mother has a habit of wake up early. Please fix the verb.

My mother has a habit of waking up early.
Why: After the preposition "of", a verb takes the -ing form.
The wedding will be held at the next Sunday. Fix this.

The wedding will be held next Sunday.
Why: Phrases with "next" take no preposition or article before them.
I am very afraid from dogs since my childhood. Two things are wrong, I think.

I have been very afraid of dogs since my childhood.
Why: The adjective takes "afraid of", not "from". "Since" with a state that continues needs the present perfect.
It's very much hot today, isn't it? Is "very much" right here?

It's very hot today, isn't it?
Why: "Very much" is not used before an adjective. Use "very" or "so".
we visited delhi, agra and jaipur in december. What needs capitals?

We visited Delhi, Agra and Jaipur in December.
Why: Capital letters are used for the first word of a sentence, names of places and names of months.
After the rain stopped, the children ran outside to play. Is the comma right?

It reads well as it is.
Why: A comma usually follows an opening clause such as "After the rain stopped".
I am tired to hear Ananya's excuses every day. Please correct.

I am tired of hearing Ananya's excuses every day.
Why: The adjective "tired" takes "of", and a verb after a preposition takes the -ing form.
Nobody have called me since morning. What should the verb be?

Nobody has called me since morning.
Why: "Nobody" is singular, so the verb is "has".
She plays the cricket and the football for her college. Any extra words?

She plays cricket and football for her college.
Why: Names of sports usually take no article.

Hey Karan long time no see how are you doing
I typed this fast. Add the punctuation please.

Hey Karan, long time no see! How are you doing?
Why: A comma separates the name of the person you address, and each separate sentence needs its own ending mark.
I'm looking for a shirt like this one but in bigger size. What is missing?

I'm looking for a shirt like this one but in a bigger size.
Why: "Size" is a singular countable noun here, so it needs "a" before it.
In spite of the rain, we played football. Is "in spite of" correct?

Yes, it is correct as it stands.
Why: "In spite of" is followed directly by a noun. "Despite" has the same meaning but takes no "of".
The enviroment club planted fifty trees near the playground. Spelling?

The environment club planted fifty trees near the playground.
Why: "Environment" has "n" before "m" in the middle: environ-ment.
I sended the file yesterday, but you didn't received it. Fix both verbs please.

I sent the file yesterday, but you didn't receive it.
Why: "Send" is irregular, and its past is "sent". After "didn't", the verb stays in the base form.
We buyed fresh fish from the harbour this morning. What is wrong?

We bought fresh fish from the harbour this morning.
Why: "Buy" is an irregular verb, and its past tense is "bought".
The sun rised at six, and the birds begin to sing. Please correct the tenses.

The sun rose at six, and the birds began to sing.
Why: The past of "rise" is "rose". Both actions happened in the past, so the second verb must also be past: "began".
The teacher divided the class in four groups for the quiz. Is "in" right?

The teacher divided the class into four groups for the quiz.
Why: When something is split into parts, the preposition is "into".
Please revert back to me by evening. Is that the right phrase?

Please reply to me by evening.
Why: "Revert back" is common in Indian workplace English, but "revert" already includes the idea of "back" and in wider English it usually means returning to an earlier state. "Reply" or "get back to me" is clearer for all readers.
Many peoples borrow money from there friends. Check this.

Many people borrow money from their friends.
Why: "People" is already plural. "Their" shows whose friends they are, while "there" points to a place.
Priya is my friend which lives near the park. Which word should I use?

Priya is my friend who lives near the park.
Why: Use "who" for people and "which" for things.
The festival is celebrated in every year in the month of March. Please tidy this up.

The festival is celebrated every year in March.
Why: Phrases with "every" take no preposition. "In March" already names the month, so "the month of" is not needed.
He kicked the ball hard and it hitted the post. Fix the verb.

He kicked the ball hard and it hit the post.
Why: "Hit" is irregular and has the same form in the past tense.
I caught cold after getting wet in the rain. Do I need an article?

I caught a cold after getting wet in the rain.
Why: "Catch a cold" is the usual modern phrase, where "a cold" is a countable illness. "Caught cold" is older and less common.
I have read this novel for three times. Is "for" needed?

I have read this novel three times.
Why: A number of times is stated without "for". Use "for" only with a length of time.
The singers voice filled the whole hall. Anything missing?

The singer's voice filled the whole hall.
Why: An apostrophe plus -s shows that the voice belongs to the singer.
Let's play a game of cards, and loser buys the snacks. What did I leave out?

Let's play a game of cards, and the loser buys the snacks.
Why: "Loser" is a singular countable noun here, so it needs "the" before it.
I forget my password, so I cannot login. Please fix.

I forgot my password, so I cannot log in.
Why: The forgetting is finished, so use the past "forgot". "Login" is a noun, and the verb is written as two words, "log in".
Heavy rains caused floods in many part of the state. Check the noun.

Heavy rains caused floods in many parts of the state.
Why: "Many" goes with a plural noun, so "part" must be "parts".
I sleep at ten and wake up at six every days. What is wrong?

I sleep at ten and wake up at six every day.
Why: "Every" is followed by a singular noun, so it is "every day".
There is a big garden in front the library. A word is missing, right?

There is a big garden in front of the library.
Why: Yes, the phrase is "in front of", so "of" is missing.
These shoes are costing too much, so I will buy other one. Please correct.

These shoes cost too much, so I will buy another one.
Why: "Cost" describes a fixed price, so it is not usually used in the continuous form. With "one", the word is "another", not "other".
The twins looks exactly like each others. Two errors, I think.

The twins look exactly like each other.
Why: "Twins" is plural, so the verb is "look". "Each other" is a fixed phrase with no -s.
The train was late for two hours. Is the phrase right?

The train was two hours late.
Why: When you give the amount, it goes before "late": "two hours late".
I wish I were taller. Should it be "was"?

It is already right.
Why: After "wish", standard English uses "were" for an imagined situation. "Was" is common in casual speech.
My sister-in-law is a bank manager. Check the hyphen and article.

Your wording works.
Why: "Sister-in-law" is written with hyphens, and "a" is right before "bank", which begins with a consonant sound.
Whoever finishes first gets the prize. Is "whoever" okay?

That reads correctly.
Why: "Whoever" is the subject of "finishes", so it is the right form, and the verb is singular.
I met an old friend in the market after long time. Missing something?

I met an old friend in the market after a long time.
Why: Yes, "a" is missing. "A long time" is the usual phrase.
The committee has announced its decision. Should it be "have"?

Good as it is.
Why: "Committee" takes "has" when it is seen as one body, as "its decision" shows. British English also allows "have" when the members are thought of one by one.
She gave to me a beautiful scarf on my birthday. Help me with the order.

She gave me a beautiful scarf on my birthday.
Why: Without "to", the person receiving comes right after "gave". With "to" it would follow: "gave a scarf to me".
The band played for two hours without to stop. Is "without to stop" okay?

The band played for two hours without stopping.
Why: After a preposition such as "without", the verb takes -ing, not "to".
She bought a leather brown bag at the fair. What would you change?

She bought a brown leather bag at the fair.
Why: Adjectives usually go in this order: colour before material.
My favourite fruits are mangoes, grapes, and, bananas. Check the commas.

My favourite fruits are mangoes, grapes, and bananas.
Why: In a list, no comma follows "and". A comma before "and" is optional, and some writers leave it out.
Fresh mango's are available at this shop. What about the apostrophe?

Fresh mangoes are available at this shop.
Why: A plural noun takes no apostrophe. The plural of "mango" is usually "mangoes".
Please write your adress and phone number on the form. Spelling?

Please write your address and phone number on the form.
Why: "Address" is spelled with a double d and a double s.
Becuase of the strike, the schools remained closed. Is "becuase" right?

Because of the strike, the schools remained closed.
Why: The spelling is b-e-c-a-u-s-e, with "au" before "se".
I will wait untill you finish writting your letter. Two spellings are wrong.

I will wait until you finish writing your letter.
Why: "Until" has only one l at the end. "Writing" drops the e of "write" and does not double the t.
The goverment has opened a new library in our town. Is it spelled right?

The government has opened a new library in our town.
Why: The word is made from "govern" plus "-ment", so the "n" stays before the "m".
Its a wierd rule that nobody can explain. Check both words.

It's a weird rule that nobody can explain.
Why: "It's" is short for "it is". "Weird" is one of the words that break the rule "i before e".
Please do a photo of us near the fountain. Can you correct?

Please take a photo of us near the fountain.
Why: The usual phrase is "take a photo". "Do" does not go with photos.
I saw a good dream last night. Is "saw" okay?

I had a good dream last night.
Why: The natural phrase for dreams is "have a dream". "See a dream" is not usual.
She gave her board exam last week. Please check the verb.

She took her board exam last week.
Why: In standard English a student "takes" an exam, while the teacher "gives" it. "Give an exam" for a student is common in India but may confuse other readers.
She hanged the wet clothes on the balcony. Is "hanged" the right past form?

She hung the wet clothes on the balcony.
Why: For objects, the past of "hang" is "hung". "Hanged" is used only for executing a person.
Let's do a picnic near the lake on Saturday. Please fix the verb.

Let's have a picnic near the lake on Saturday.
Why: A picnic is something we "have" or "go on". We do not "do" one.
When I was a child, I am afraid of the dark. Please correct.

When I was a child, I was afraid of the dark.
Why: The time is "when I was a child", so the main verb must also be in the past.
Where did you used to live before? Is "used" okay?

Where did you use to live before?
Why: After "did", the main verb is in the base form, so "used to" becomes "use to".
I have a doubt in this sum. Can you explain it?

I have a question about this sum. Can you explain it?
Why: In Indian English "I have a doubt" is a common way to ask a question. In international English "doubt" means feeling unsure, so "question" is clearer. We ask a question "about" a topic.
This books are mine, and that one are yours. Please check.

These books are mine, and that one is yours.
Why: "These" goes with plural nouns, and "that one" is singular, so it takes "is".
Two of the childs were crying in the park. Is the plural right?

Two of the children were crying in the park.
Why: "Child" has an irregular plural, "children".
My niece lost two tooths this month. What is the plural?

My niece lost two teeth this month.
Why: "Tooth" is irregular. Its plural is "teeth".
My cousin studies in an university in Pune. Which article is right?

My cousin studies at a university in Pune.
Why: "University" starts with a "yoo" sound, which is a consonant sound, so it takes "a". "Studies at" is the usual wording for a college or university.
We discussed about the new project in the office meeting. Anything extra?

We discussed the new project in the office meeting.
Why: "Discuss" takes its object directly, with no "about".
Her handwriting is same as mine. What is missing?

Her handwriting is the same as mine.
Why: "Same" needs "the" before it.
The soup tastes badly without salt. Is "badly" correct?

The soup tastes bad without salt.
Why: After a verb like "taste", use an adjective that describes the soup, not an adverb.
Add little salt and stir till the sugar dissolve. Is there anything to fix?

Add a little salt and stir till the sugar dissolves.
Why: "A little" means a small amount, while "little" alone means almost none. "Sugar" is singular, so the verb is "dissolves".
A peacock is a national bird of India. Do I need "the"?

The peacock is the national bird of India.
Why: There is only one national bird, so it takes "the". Naming the kind of bird with "the peacock" is also usual.
I reach school before the bell rings, so I never late. Something is missing, isn't it?

I reach school before the bell rings, so I am never late.
Why: Yes, the verb "am" is missing. An adjective like "late" needs a linking verb, and "never" goes after "am".
The guide explained us the history of the fort. How should I word this?

The guide explained the history of the fort to us.
Why: "Explain" takes the thing explained first, and the person comes after "to".
She felt very embarassed when she forgot her lines. Is the spelling right?

She felt very embarrassed when she forgot her lines.
Why: "Embarrassed" is spelled with a double r and a double s.
My uncle's son is my cousin brother. Is that the right term?

My uncle's son is my cousin.
Why: "Cousin" already covers both boys and girls. "Cousin brother" is used in India but is not standard English elsewhere.
Can I take a leave tomorrow? My cousin is getting married.

Can I take leave tomorrow? My cousin is getting married.
Why: In international English "leave" meaning time off work is usually uncountable, so it takes no "a". Indian English often says "a leave". "Take a day off" is another natural option.
The batsman hit the ball so hardly that it went over the fence. Fix the adverb.

The batsman hit the ball so hard that it went over the fence.
Why: "Hard" is used both as an adjective and as an adverb. "Hardly" means "almost not".
He earns less than I do, but he saves more as I do. Anything off?

He earns less than I do, but he saves more than I do.
Why: "More" is followed by "than" in a comparison, not "as".
I am allergic from peanuts, so I read every label. Which word is wrong?

I am allergic to peanuts, so I read every label.
Why: The adjective "allergic" is followed by "to".
The story, which I read last night, was so touching that I almost cried. Are the commas correct?

Everything is in place.
Why: The commas set off "which I read last night" as extra information, and "so ... that" correctly links the result.
My room is smaller than my sister. What should I change?

My room is smaller than my sister's.
Why: The sentence compares two rooms, so it needs "my sister's", meaning her room. Otherwise it compares a room with a person.
The rangoli looked very beautifully, so everybody took photos. Fix please.

The rangoli looked very beautiful, so everybody took photos.
Why: After "looked" meaning "seemed", we use an adjective, not an adverb.
Fish lives in water and breathe through gills. What is wrong?

Fish live in water and breathe through gills.
Why: In this general sense "fish" is plural, with the same form as the singular, so the verb is "live" like "breathe".
Water boils at 100 degree Celsius at sea level. Is "degree" right?

Water boils at 100 degrees Celsius at sea level.
Why: After a number larger than one, the noun is plural: "degrees".
My mother tongue is Tamil, and I can also speak Hindi and a little English. Is this correct?

No errors here.
Why: "A little English" correctly means some English, and "can also speak" is in the usual order.
The prize distribution will held in the school hall. Please correct.

The prize distribution will be held in the school hall.
Why: A passive form needs "be" plus the past participle, so it is "will be held".
Thank you for the lovely gift, it was very kind off you. Please fix this note.

Thank you for the lovely gift. It was very kind of you.
Why: The phrase is "kind of you", not "off". Also, two complete sentences are better separated with a full stop.
Neha is as taller as her brother. Which word is wrong?

Neha is as tall as her brother.
Why: In "as ... as", the adjective stays in its plain form, "tall".
My neighbours are going on a trip, so I will water they plants. Check the pronoun.

My neighbours are going on a trip, so I will water their plants.
Why: Before a noun we need the possessive "their". "They" is the subject form.
Please open your books at the page twenty. Is "the" needed?

Please open your books at page twenty.
Why: A page number is used without "the". Many speakers also say "on page twenty".
Let us make two teams and played a quick match. What is wrong with the verb?

Let us make two teams and play a quick match.
Why: After "let us", both verbs stay in the base form.
The password should contain atleast eight characters. Is "atleast" one word?

The password should contain at least eight characters.
Why: "At least" is written as two words.
I usually have my dinner at the 8 o'clock. Is "the" correct?

I usually have my dinner at 8 o'clock.
Why: A clock time takes no "the" in front of it.
He eats the lunch at school and the dinner at home. Any extra words?

He eats lunch at school and dinner at home.
Why: Names of meals usually take no article when we speak of them in general.
I can't afford buy this phone yet. Please correct.

I can't afford to buy this phone yet.
Why: "Afford" is followed by "to" plus the base verb.
It has stopped raining, so we can go out. Is "stopped raining" okay?

It reads fine.
Why: The present perfect "has stopped" links the past to now, and "stop" plus -ing correctly means the rain ended.
I have been collecting coins since I was nine. Is the tense okay?

Looks right.
Why: "Since" with a past starting point takes the present perfect continuous, and "was nine" is the correct simple past for that starting point.
We arrived at the station early, so we waited in the cafe. Is "arrived at" right?

Your sentence stands as written.
Why: We "arrive at" a station, and "waited in the cafe" places them inside the cafe.
Hardly had we reached the ground when it began to rain. Is the order right?

Yes, the order is right.
Why: A sentence that begins with "Hardly" puts the helper "had" before the subject, and "when" completes the pattern.
My neighbour's daughter is learning to dance. Is the apostrophe right?

Nothing is wrong.
Why: The apostrophe plus -s shows the daughter belongs to one neighbour, and "learning to dance" uses "to" with a base verb.
We need three things; a brush, a canvas and some paint for the art class. Check the punctuation.

We need three things: a brush, a canvas and some paint for the art class.
Why: A colon introduces a list. A semicolon is not used for this.
She has a three years old son. What should change?

She has a three-year-old son.
Why: A compound adjective before a noun is joined with hyphens, and its unit stays singular: "year".
She wore a red saree for the special occassion. Is the spelling right?

She wore a red saree for the special occasion.
Why: "Occasion" is spelled with a double c but only one s.
We planted tomatos and potatos in the garden. Correct the plurals.

We planted tomatoes and potatoes in the garden.
Why: Many nouns ending in -o, such as "tomato" and "potato", add -es in the plural.
It was an intresting talk on the history of our town. Spelling?

It was an interesting talk on the history of our town.
Why: "Interesting" has an "e" after the "r": inter-est-ing.
The classroom was so quite that you could hear the clock. Is "quite" the right word?

The classroom was so quiet that you could hear the clock.
Why: "Quiet" means making little noise. "Quite" means fairly or very.
I will go for a walk if it won't rain this evening. Is "won't" right?

I will go for a walk if it doesn't rain this evening.
Why: In an "if" clause about the future, the present tense is used, so "doesn't rain" replaces "won't rain".
Stop to shout, the neighbours can hear you. Please fix.

Stop shouting. The neighbours can hear you.
Why: "Stop" plus -ing means ending the action. "Stop to shout" would mean pausing in order to shout. Two full sentences should also be split with a full stop.
The driver speaks that the bus will be late. Is "speaks" right?

The driver says that the bus will be late.
Why: "Say" is used for reporting words. "Speak" is for talking in general or in a language.
He is on the top of the world after winning the award. Is the idiom right?

He is on top of the world after winning the award.
Why: The idiom is "on top of the world", with no "the" before "top".
Please give back me the book by Friday. Is the word order right?

Please give me back the book by Friday.
Why: The person comes right after "give", so "me" goes before "back". You can also say "give the book back to me".
Some of my cousin are visiting us in May. Fix the grammar.

Some of my cousins are visiting us in May.
Why: After "some of my", the noun is plural, and the verb "are" agrees with it.
I have seen already this film. What should I move?

I have already seen this film.
Why: "Already" usually goes between the helper "have" and the past participle "seen".
Moon goes around Earth once a month. Does it need articles?

The Moon goes around the Earth once a month.
Why: "Moon" takes "the" here. "The Earth" is the usual form in this sense, though "Earth" alone is also used in science.
Rina and Tom gave theirselves a short break after the walk. Is "theirselves" a word?

Rina and Tom gave themselves a short break after the walk.
Why: The reflexive pronoun for "they" is "themselves". "Theirselves" is not used in standard English.
The exam results will be announced next week. Is "will be announced" right?

That is fine.
Why: The passive "will be announced" suits a result that people receive, and "next week" needs no preposition.
Most of the milk have been spilled on the floor. Which verb is right?

Most of the milk has been spilled on the floor.
Why: After "most of", the verb agrees with the noun that follows. "Milk" is uncountable and takes a singular verb.
There is no point to argue with him about it. Fix the verb form.

There is no point in arguing with him about it.
Why: The phrase is "no point in" followed by an -ing form.
The wind blew the leafs off the tree. What is the plural?

The wind blew the leaves off the tree.
Why: Nouns such as "leaf" change -f to -ves in the plural.
If he would have told me about the quiz, I would have prepared. Can you check the conditional?

If he had told me about the quiz, I would have prepared.
Why: In a third conditional the if-clause takes the past perfect ("had told"). "Would have" belongs only in the result clause.
I wish I would have studied harder for the exam last week. Is this the right form?

I wish I had studied harder for the exam last week.
Why: To wish about the past, use the past perfect ("had studied"), not "would have".
It's time we leave, or we will miss the bus. What is off in the first part?

It's time we left, or we will miss the bus.
Why: After "it's time" plus a subject, the verb is usually in the past simple ("left"), even though the time to act is now.
I'd rather you don't tell anyone about the surprise party. Does the verb need changing?

I'd rather you didn't tell anyone about the surprise party.
Why: After "I'd rather" plus a new subject, English uses the past form ("didn't") to talk about the present or future.
Would you mind if I open the window? It is very warm in here. Please polish the request.

Would you mind if I opened the window? It is very warm in here.
Why: A polite "Would you mind if I ..." is followed by the past simple.
If only I know the answer to the last clue, we would win the quiz. Tell me what to fix.

If only I knew the answer to the last clue, we would win the quiz.
Why: "If only" about an unreal present takes the past form ("knew"), which also matches "would win".
I had gone to Delhi last year for a wedding. Is "had gone" the right tense?

I went to Delhi last year for a wedding.
Why: Use the simple past for a finished event with a time like "last year". The past perfect is for something that happened before another past event.
While I was walking home, I have seen a rainbow over the hills. Please fix the verb.

While I was walking home, I saw a rainbow over the hills.
Why: A single finished event in a past story takes the simple past. "Have seen" does not fit a narrated past.
When the rain stopped, we are going out to play cricket. Please make the tenses agree.

When the rain stopped, we went out to play cricket.
Why: "Stopped" is past, so the main verb must also be in a past form ("went").
Our teacher told us that the Earth goes around the Sun. Should "goes" be "went" after "told"?

No, "goes" is right as it is.
Why: A fact that is always true can stay in the present tense even after a past verb such as "told".
My brother pretended being asleep when the guests arrived. Please correct.

My brother pretended to be asleep when the guests arrived.
Why: "Pretend" is followed by "to + verb", not an -ing form.
I'm considering to change my bank next month. Which verb form is right?

I'm considering changing my bank next month.
Why: "Consider" is followed by an -ing form.
They postponed to hold the meeting until Monday. Can you fix this?

They postponed holding the meeting until Monday.
Why: "Postpone" takes an -ing form, not "to + verb".
I can't help to laugh when he tells that story. What should I change?

I can't help laughing when he tells that story.
Why: "Can't help" is followed by an -ing form.
We managed finishing the report before the deadline. Please look at the verb.

We managed to finish the report before the deadline.
Why: "Manage" is followed by "to + verb".
My aunt gave up to knit sweaters when her eyes grew weak. What is the right form?

My aunt gave up knitting sweaters when her eyes grew weak.
Why: "Give up" is followed by an -ing form.
The old fort is worth to visit if you have a free afternoon. Is "worth to visit" right?

The old fort is worth visiting if you have a free afternoon.
Why: "Worth" takes an -ing form, not "to + verb".
I saw a monkey to snatch a banana from the vendor. Please correct it.

I saw a monkey snatch a banana from the vendor.
Why: After "saw" plus an object, use the plain verb (or an -ing form for an action in progress), not "to".
I prefer tea than coffee in the morning. Is "than" right here?

I prefer tea to coffee in the morning.
Why: With "prefer", compare two things with "to". "Than" is used with comparatives such as "better than".
I feel like to go out for a long walk after this rain. Check the verb, please.

I feel like going out for a long walk after this rain.
Why: "Feel like" is followed by an -ing form.
She sat in the front of me in the cinema hall and blocked my view. Which phrase is wrong?

She sat in front of me in the cinema hall and blocked my view.
Why: "In front of" means directly ahead of someone. "In the front of" means the front part of a place or thing.
They are sitting at the bench near the fountain. Is the preposition right?

They are sitting on the bench near the fountain.
Why: People usually sit "on" a bench; "at" is used for a table or desk.
The camp is between 5 to 10 December. Something is wrong with the pair of words.

The camp is between 5 and 10 December.
Why: "Between" is paired with "and", and "from" is paired with "to". "Between ... to" mixes the two pairs.
We stayed with our cousins during three days. Should I use "for" instead?

We stayed with our cousins for three days.
Why: Use "for" with a length of time. "During" goes with an event or a period, as in "during the holidays".
The injury prevented him to play in the final. Please check the end.

The injury prevented him from playing in the final.
Why: "Prevent someone" is followed by "from + -ing".
She was blamed of breaking the vase, though it was the cat. What is wrong?

She was blamed for breaking the vase, though it was the cat.
Why: The usual phrase is "blame someone for" something.
Everyone should be aware about the new rules for the lab. Is "aware about" okay?

Everyone should be aware of the new rules for the lab.
Why: "Aware" is followed by "of".
The answer of this question is in the second chapter. Do I need a different word?

The answer to this question is in the second chapter.
Why: The usual phrase is "the answer to" a question.
What is the reason of the delay in the courier? Please correct it.

What is the reason for the delay in the courier?
Why: "Reason" is followed by "for".
My mother asked me what was my plan for the weekend. Is the word order right?

My mother asked me what my plan for the weekend was.
Why: A reported question uses statement order, so the subject "my plan" comes before the verb "was".
The manager wanted to know that where I had worked before. Please tidy this up.

The manager wanted to know where I had worked before.
Why: A reported question needs no "that" before the question word.
I wonder what is he doing in the garden so early. Fix the order, please.

I wonder what he is doing in the garden so early.
Why: After "I wonder", the embedded question uses statement word order: subject, then verb.
She asked me that what I was doing there. Which word should go?

She asked me what I was doing there.
Why: A reported question has no "that" in front of the question word.
He asked me where I was going? Is the question mark needed?

He asked me where I was going.
Why: A reported question is a statement, so it ends with a full stop, not a question mark.
The teacher asked who had broken the window, but nobody answered. Is the reported question correct?

Yes, that's right.
Why: A reported question keeps statement word order, and "had broken" rightly shows the act came before the asking.
Everything what he said in the speech was true. Is "what" the right word?

Everything that he said in the speech was true.
Why: After "everything", the linking word is "that" (or nothing at all), not "what".
The person to who I spoke on the phone was very helpful. Check the relative word.

The person to whom I spoke on the phone was very helpful.
Why: After a preposition, the relative pronoun is "whom". In everyday speech people say "the person who I spoke to".
This is the house where I was born in. Can you fix the end?

This is the house where I was born.
Why: "Where" already means "in which", so the extra "in" repeats it.
The reason why he left is because he felt ignored. Does this sound right?

The reason why he left is that he felt ignored.
Why: The usual pattern is "the reason ... is that". "Is because" repeats the idea of reason, though it is common in speech.
I gave my landlord two weeks notice before moving out. Fix the apostrophe.

I gave my landlord two weeks' notice before moving out.
Why: Expressions of time that work like possessives take an apostrophe: "two weeks' notice".
Her favourite songs were all from the 1990's. Is the apostrophe needed?

Her favourite songs were all from the 1990s.
Why: A plural for a decade is just -s. An apostrophe is not needed.
Somebody's else umbrella is lying in the hall. Where does the apostrophe go?

Somebody else's umbrella is lying in the hall.
Why: With phrases like "somebody else", the possessive 's goes on the last word.
This is Charles's bicycle, not Priya's. Is it "Charles's" or "Charles'"?

Both forms are acceptable, so your sentence is fine.
Why: Singular names ending in -s can take 's or just an apostrophe. Style guides differ, so pick one and keep to it.
My birthday is in april, and my sister's is on a sunday. Which words need capitals?

My birthday is in April, and my sister's is on a Sunday.
Why: Names of months and days of the week always start with a capital letter.
I told My Mother and Father about the trip. Do those need capitals?

I told my mother and father about the trip.
Why: After a possessive like "my", words such as "mother" are lowercase. They take capitals only when used as names, as in "Mother said so".
Dr. Mehta is a Doctor, and his wife is a Professor at the university. Check the capitals.

Dr. Mehta is a doctor, and his wife is a professor at the university.
Why: A job word is capitalised only as part of a title before a name, such as "Professor Rao". Used as a common noun it is lowercase.
We drove South along the coast and reached Goa in the evening. Is "South" right?

We drove south along the coast and reached Goa in the evening.
Why: Compass directions are lowercase unless they are part of a name, such as "South India".
On Teacher's day, we gave our class teacher flowers. Please fix the festival name.

On Teachers' Day, we gave our class teacher flowers.
Why: Names of special days are capitalised. "Teachers'" is the plural possessive, because the day is for all teachers.
Let's go for a walk after dinner, don't we? Is the tag right?

Let's go for a walk after dinner, shall we?
Why: The tag for "let's" is "shall we?".
Nobody noticed the mistake, didn't they? Check the end of it.

Nobody noticed the mistake, did they?
Why: "Nobody" has a negative meaning, so the tag is positive: "did they?".
My friend is from Netherlands and speaks perfect Dutch. Does the country name need anything?

My friend is from the Netherlands and speaks perfect Dutch.
Why: A few country names, such as the Netherlands and the Philippines, take "the".
We flew over Atlantic Ocean for nine hours. Please check the articles.

We flew over the Atlantic Ocean for nine hours.
Why: Names of oceans, seas and rivers take "the".
Tourists love to walk across Howrah Bridge at sunset. Is an article missing?

No change is needed. "Howrah Bridge" is correct as written.
Why: Many bridge names, such as Howrah Bridge and Tower Bridge, are normally used without "the". Some, such as "the Brooklyn Bridge", usually take it, so usage varies.
Mr. Iyer is a principal of our school and teaches maths too. Which article is right?

Mr. Iyer is the principal of our school and teaches maths too.
Why: A school has only one principal, so the definite article "the" is the natural choice.
She is one of the my closest friends from college. Fix the extra word.

She is one of my closest friends from college.
Why: A possessive such as "my" already points to the noun, so "the" is not added.
She is an European visitor and has never tasted dosa. Please correct the article.

She is a European visitor and has never tasted dosa.
Why: The choice of "a" or "an" depends on the sound. "European" begins with a "y" sound, so it takes "a".
The Ganga and the Yamuna meet at Prayagraj. Are the articles right for the rivers?

Yes, they are right.
Why: River names take "the", and a city name such as Prayagraj does not.
I have drank two glasses of water since I woke up. Which form of "drink" is right?

I have drunk two glasses of water since I woke up.
Why: "Drink" is irregular (drink, drank, drunk), and "have" needs the past participle "drunk".
My cousin swimmed across the lake last summer. Is "swimmed" a word?

My cousin swam across the lake last summer.
Why: "Swim" is irregular: the past simple is "swam" and the participle is "swum".
My bicycle was stole outside the market yesterday. Please fix the verb.

My bicycle was stolen outside the market yesterday.
Why: After "was" in the passive, use the past participle: steal, stole, stolen.
The match has began, so please hurry to your seats. What is the right verb form?

The match has begun, so please hurry to your seats.
Why: "Begin" is irregular (begin, began, begun), and "has" needs the participle "begun".
I will can join you after the meeting next week. Is "will can" allowed?

I will be able to join you after the meeting next week.
Why: "Can" has no future form and cannot follow "will". Use "will be able to".
You had better to leave now if you want to catch the train. Fix the verb.

You had better leave now if you want to catch the train.
Why: "Had better" is followed by the plain verb, with no "to".
You needn't to bring anything; we have everything. What is wrong?

You needn't bring anything; we have everything.
Why: The modal "needn't" is followed by the plain verb, with no "to".
A strange thing was happened at the fair yesterday. Please correct this.

A strange thing happened at the fair yesterday.
Why: "Happen" does not take an object, so it cannot be used in the passive.
The temple near our house built in 1950 and is still used. Something is missing.

The temple near our house was built in 1950 and is still used.
Why: A passive verb needs "was" (or another form of "be") before the participle "built".
Not only he is clever, but also kind to everyone. Check the word order.

Not only is he clever, but also kind to everyone.
Why: After "not only" at the start of a sentence, the helper verb comes before the subject. Adding "he is" before "also" would be a little more formal.
Never I have seen such a crowded station before. Is the order right?

Never have I seen such a crowded station before.
Why: When a negative adverb such as "never" starts a sentence, the helper verb comes before the subject. This is mostly used in formal writing.
I don't like horror movies too. Should "too" be changed?

I don't like horror movies either.
Why: In a negative sentence, use "either" instead of "too".
I don't have enough of money to buy this watch. Do I need "of"?

I don't have enough money to buy this watch.
Why: Before a plain noun, "enough" is used directly with no "of".
The scientist did many researches on bees in the garden. Please correct.

The scientist did a lot of research on bees in the garden.
Why: "Research" is usually uncountable, so it has no plural and does not go with "many". Use "a lot of" instead.
The detective in this novel found many evidences in the old kitchen. What is wrong?

The detective in this novel found a lot of evidence in the old kitchen.
Why: "Evidence" is uncountable, so it takes no plural -s and does not go with "many".
She bought two breads and a packet of butter from the shop. Please fix the first noun.

She bought two loaves of bread and a packet of butter from the shop.
Why: "Bread" is uncountable, so count it with a unit such as "loaves" or "slices".
He gave us a lot of knowledges about the ancient coins. Is "knowledges" a word?

He gave us a lot of knowledge about the ancient coins.
Why: "Knowledge" is uncountable and has no plural form.
Ten kilometres are a long way to walk with heavy bags. Should the verb be "is"?

Ten kilometres is a long way to walk with heavy bags.
Why: A distance, amount or period of time is treated as one unit, so it takes a singular verb.
One-third of the students was absent on Monday. Check the verb.

One-third of the students were absent on Monday.
Why: With a fraction, the verb agrees with the noun after "of". "Students" is plural, so "were".
My mother, not my brothers, are going to the wedding. Which verb is right?

My mother, not my brothers, is going to the wedding.
Why: In "X, not Y", the verb agrees with the first subject, "my mother".
Bread and butter is my usual breakfast. Why is it "is" and not "are"?

The sentence is correct as it stands.
Why: When two nouns form one dish or idea, they usually take a singular verb. "Are" would suit them if they were thought of as separate items.
Either of the buses go to the station. Is "go" right?

Either of the buses goes to the station.
Why: "Either of" is followed by a singular verb in careful English.
This bag is twice more expensive than that one. Fix the comparison.

This bag is twice as expensive as that one.
Why: "Twice" goes with "as ... as", not with "more ... than".
I will call you tommorow and bring the notes. Please correct the spelling.

I will call you tomorrow and bring the notes.
Why: "Tomorrow" has a single m and a double r.
We booked accomodation near the beach for three nights. Is the spelling right?

We booked accommodation near the beach for three nights.
Why: "Accommodation" has a double c and a double m.
My freind lives near the temple and walks past our house every day. Check the spelling.

My friend lives near the temple and walks past our house every day.
Why: "Friend" is spelled with "ie", as in "fiend" with an r added.
She is a very sucessful singer and tours every winter. Is there a spelling error?

She is a very successful singer and tours every winter.
Why: "Successful" has a double c and a double s.
Her buisness sells handmade soaps and candles. Fix the spelling, please.

Her business sells handmade soaps and candles.
Why: "Business" is spelled bus-i-ness, built from "busy" with the y changed to i.
Please write the sentance on the board. How is this word spelled?

Please write the sentence on the board.
Why: "Sentence" ends in "-ence", not "-ance".
I do excercise in the garden every morning. Is it spelled right?

I do exercise in the garden every morning.
Why: "Exercise" is spelled ex-er-cise, with no "c" after the x.
What is the lenght of this rope? Please correct the spelling.

What is the length of this rope?
Why: "Length" ends in "-gth", not "-nth".
He plays the guitar well, and his sister sings beautifull. Fix the last word.

He plays the guitar well, and his sister sings beautifully.
Why: An adverb is made with -ly. "Beautiful" plus "ly" gives "beautifully", with a double l at the end.
Thier teacher gave them extra time for the test. Is this spelled right?

Their teacher gave them extra time for the test.
Why: "Their" is spelled with "ei". It shows ownership, as in "their teacher".
Everyone enjoyed the lunch accept the cold soup. Is "accept" the right word?

Everyone enjoyed the lunch except the cold soup.
Why: "Except" means "not including", while "accept" means "to receive or agree to".
My teacher gave me a complement on my handwriting. Which spelling is right?

My teacher gave me a compliment on my handwriting.
Why: A "compliment" is a kind word of praise. "Complement" means something that completes another.
He read the poem allowed to the whole class. Is "allowed" the right word?

He read the poem aloud to the whole class.
Why: "Aloud" means out loud. "Allowed" means permitted.
A polar bare walked across the ice in the video. Which word is wrong?

A polar bear walked across the ice in the video.
Why: "Bear" is the animal. "Bare" means uncovered.
Please don't waist water while washing the car. Check the spelling.

Please don't waste water while washing the car.
Why: "Waste" means to use carelessly. "Waist" is the middle of the body.
She said "I am tired and want to rest". Please fix the punctuation.

She said, "I am tired and want to rest."
Why: A comma usually introduces a spoken quotation, and the full stop goes inside the closing quotation mark.
I like tea; but my brother likes coffee. Is the semicolon right?

I like tea, but my brother likes coffee.
Why: A semicolon joins two sentences without a joining word. When "but" is used, a comma goes before it.
Because it was raining, we stayed home and played cards. Do I need a comma after "raining"?

Yes, your comma is right.
Why: A comma usually follows an opening "because" clause before the main clause begins.
Can we prepone the meeting to Thursday? Is "prepone" a real word?

Yes, it is a real word in Indian English, but many readers elsewhere do not know it. A version that works everywhere: Can we bring the meeting forward to Thursday?
Why: "Prepone" is the opposite of "postpone" in Indian English. "Bring forward" is understood in every variety.
The bank is opposite to the school on this road. Is "opposite to" okay?

The bank is opposite the school on this road.
Why: As a preposition, "opposite" needs no "to". "Opposite to" is common in Indian English, but the shorter form is standard.
Walking to school, a dog chased me. Does the opening phrase work?

Walking to school, I was chased by a dog.
Why: An opening phrase describes the subject that follows it. In the original, "a dog" seems to be walking, so "I" must become the subject.
I bought a cake for my mother with chocolate icing. Is the order of the words clear?

I bought a cake with chocolate icing for my mother.
Why: Put a describing phrase next to the noun it describes, so "with chocolate icing" stays with "cake" and not "mother".
The boy was hit by a ball wearing a red cap. Something sounds odd to me.

The boy wearing a red cap was hit by a ball.
Why: "Wearing a red cap" should sit next to "the boy". Where it was, it seemed to describe the ball.
Covered in dust, I cleaned the old bookshelf. Does that describe the right thing?

I cleaned the old bookshelf, which was covered in dust.
Why: An opening phrase describes the subject, so the original says that "I" was covered in dust. The relative clause attaches the dust to the bookshelf.
I couldn't find my ticket nowhere in the bag. What is wrong?

I couldn't find my ticket anywhere in the bag.
Why: "Couldn't" and "nowhere" are both negative, which makes a double negative. After a negative verb, use "anywhere".
She hardly never misses a class. Is "hardly never" right?

She hardly ever misses a class.
Why: "Hardly" already has a negative meaning, so "never" is not added. The usual phrase is "hardly ever".
She likes coffee, isn't she? Please check the tag.

She likes coffee, doesn't she?
Why: A question tag repeats the helper verb of the main clause. "Likes" is present simple, so the tag uses "doesn't".
I am late, amn't I? Is "amn't I" correct?

I am late, aren't I?
Why: "Aren't I?" is the standard tag after "I am". "Amn't" is found only in some dialects, such as Irish and Scottish English.
You won't tell anyone about this, will you? Is the tag right after "won't"?

Yes, the tag is right.
Why: After a negative statement, the tag is positive: "won't ... will you?".
It is a long time that I saw you. How can I say this more naturally?

It has been a long time since I saw you.
Why: The usual pattern is "It has been a long time since" plus the past simple. The "that" pattern is heard in Indian English but is not standard.
I have not met my uncle since long. Is "since long" okay?

I have not met my uncle for a long time.
Why: "Since" needs a starting point, such as "since March". For a length of time, use "for". "Since long" is heard in Indian English.
My friend did friendship with a new girl in class. Which verb is wrong?

My friend made friends with a new girl in class.
Why: The usual phrase is "make friends with" someone. "Do" does not go with "friendship".
She makes exercise at the park every evening. Please correct the verb.

She does exercise at the park every evening.
Why: "Exercise" is used with "do" or "take", not "make".
I make a walk along the river after dinner. Is "make a walk" right?

I take a walk along the river after dinner.
Why: The usual phrase is "take a walk" or "go for a walk".
We made an experiment to see which cloth dries faster. Which verb is right?

We did an experiment to see which cloth dries faster.
Why: Experiments are "done" or "carried out", not "made".
She is keen in learning the veena. Is "keen in" correct?

She is keen on learning the veena.
Why: "Keen" is followed by "on" ("keen on something").
He is responsible of the school library this year. Which preposition fits?

He is responsible for the school library this year.
Why: "Responsible" is followed by "for".
She succeeded to win the gold medal after years of practice. Check the verb pattern.

She succeeded in winning the gold medal after years of practice.
Why: "Succeed in" is followed by an -ing form.
I am not familiar to this area, so please guide me. Is "familiar to" okay?

I am not familiar with this area, so please guide me.
Why: A person is "familiar with" a place. We use "to" the other way round: "The area is familiar to me".
I will get my phone to repair tomorrow. What is the right pattern?

I will get my phone repaired tomorrow.
Why: When someone else does a job for you, use "get" or "have", then the object and a past participle.
I had my bicycle repaired yesterday. Is "had my bicycle repaired" correct?

This is already correct.
Why: "Have" plus an object and a past participle correctly says that someone else did the work.
The bridge is been repaired this month. Please fix the verb.

The bridge is being repaired this month.
Why: The present continuous passive is "is being" plus the past participle.
Please pick up him at the station at six. Is the word order right?

Please pick him up at the station at six.
Why: When the object of a phrasal verb is a pronoun, it goes between the verb and the particle: "pick him up".
Where are you going today. Check my end punctuation.

Where are you going today?
Why: A direct question ends with a question mark, not a full stop.
She is a well known writer in our town. Does "well known" need a hyphen?

She is a well-known writer in our town.
Why: A compound adjective before a noun is usually written with a hyphen.
My uncle is twenty five years older than my aunt. Is there a punctuation problem?

My uncle is twenty-five years older than my aunt.
Why: Compound numbers from 21 to 99 are written with a hyphen.
My cousin is of sixteen years and plays tennis. How do I say the age correctly?

My cousin is sixteen years old and plays tennis.
Why: Age is given as "be + number (+ years old)". "Is of sixteen years" is heard in Indian English but is not standard.
Yesterday I met with an accident near the bus stand, but I am fine. Please correct.

Yesterday I had an accident near the bus stand, but I am fine.
Why: "Have an accident" is the standard phrase. "Meet with an accident" is common in Indian English and in some older writing.
How is the weather like in Shimla now? What is wrong with the question?

What is the weather like in Shimla now?
Why: "What ... like" asks for a description. "How is the weather?" also works, but "how" and "like" are not used together.
Remember to take your notebook when you come to my house tomorrow. Is "take" right?

Remember to bring your notebook when you come to my house tomorrow.
Why: "Bring" means to carry something towards the speaker's place. "Take" means to carry it away from there.
This is an economic way to travel to the city. Is "economic" the word I want?

This is an economical way to travel to the city.
Why: "Economical" means saving money. "Economic" is about the economy of a country.
She is very sensible about other people's feelings. Is "sensible" right?

She is very sensitive to other people's feelings.
Why: "Sensitive" means quick to notice feelings. "Sensible" means practical and reasonable.
The mens' hockey team won the district cup. Where does the apostrophe go?

The men's hockey team won the district cup.
Why: "Men" is already plural, so the possessive adds 's, as in "children's".
She likes cooking, to read and playing chess. Fix the list.

She likes cooking, reading and playing chess.
Why: Items in a list should have the same form. Here all three are -ing forms.
Please repeat that again, I could not hear you. Is "repeat again" needed?

Please repeat that. I could not hear you.
Why: "Repeat" already means "say again", so "again" is usually left out. A comma should not join two full sentences.
My sister works like a nurse in Pune. Is "like" right here?

My sister works as a nurse in Pune.
Why: Use "as" for a job or role. "Like" means "similar to".
Ravi is a friend of my from school. Please fix the end.

Ravi is a friend of mine from school.
Why: After "of", a possessive pronoun is used: "of mine", not "of my".
She walked in to the kitchen and opened the fridge. Is "in to" two words?

She walked into the kitchen and opened the fridge.
Why: "Into" is one word when it shows movement from outside to inside a place.
Lets meet at the bus stop at five. Fix the apostrophe, please.

Let's meet at the bus stop at five.
Why: "Let's" is short for "let us" and needs an apostrophe.
She lead the team to victory in last year's final. Is "lead" right?

She led the team to victory in last year's final.
Why: The past tense of "lead" is "led". "Lead" is the present form (or the metal).
I like to wonder around the old market on Sunday mornings. Which word is wrong?

I like to wander around the old market on Sunday mornings.
Why: "Wander" means to walk around without a plan. "Wonder" means to think or be curious.
My brother eats serial with milk every morning. Is the spelling right?

My brother eats cereal with milk every morning.
Why: "Cereal" is the grain food. "Serial" means happening in a series.
The new bridge is made of steal and concrete. Check the spelling.

The new bridge is made of steel and concrete.
Why: "Steel" is the strong metal. "Steal" means to take something that is not yours.
Whom did you invite to the party? Should it be "who" instead?

No, "whom" is correct in careful English.
Why: "Whom" is the object form of "who", and here it is the object of "invite". In casual speech, many people say "who".
She doesn't have any brothers or sisters. Is there a double negative here?

No, the sentence is correct.
Why: A double negative means two negative words in one clause. Here only "doesn't" is negative, and "any" is the right word after it.
If I have time, I would visit you on Sunday. Please check the conditional.

If I have time, I will visit you on Sunday.
Why: A real future possibility takes the present simple in the if-clause and "will" in the main clause. "Would" goes with a past form, as in "If I had time".
Those who is late must wait outside the hall. Which verb is right?

Those who are late must wait outside the hall.
Why: "Those" is plural, so "who" takes a plural verb: "are".
Neither Raj nor I am going to the fair. Does the verb agree with "I"?

Yes, "am" is correct.
Why: With "neither ... nor", the verb agrees with the subject nearest to it. That subject is "I", so "am".
The all students were happy about the holiday. What should change?

All the students were happy about the holiday.
Why: "All" comes before "the", not after it.
We stayed in instead of to go out in the rain. Please correct the end.

We stayed in instead of going out in the rain.
Why: After a preposition such as "instead of", a verb takes the -ing form.
The food was cheap. In the other hand, the service was slow. Check the phrase.

The food was cheap. On the other hand, the service was slow.
Why: The fixed phrase is "on the other hand", used to introduce a contrast.
In my point of view, school uniforms are very useful. Is "in my point of view" right?

From my point of view, school uniforms are very useful.
Why: The usual phrases are "from my point of view" and "in my view". "In my point of view" is a mix of the two.
In the end of the film, everybody clapped. Which words are wrong?

At the end of the film, everybody clapped.
Why: Use "at the end of" with a noun. "In the end" stands alone and means "finally".
According to me, the exam was easy. Is "according to me" okay?

In my opinion, the exam was easy.
Why: "According to" usually names another person or a source. For your own view, "in my opinion" is more usual, though "according to me" is heard in Indian English.
The teacher emphasised on neat handwriting in all subjects. What should I change?

The teacher emphasised neat handwriting in all subjects.
Why: "Emphasise" takes its object directly, with no "on".
All parents must attend to the meeting on Friday. Is "attend to" right?

All parents must attend the meeting on Friday.
Why: "Attend" takes its object directly when it means to be present at an event. "Attend to" means to deal with something.
In case it will rain, take an umbrella. Please check the verb.

In case it rains, take an umbrella.
Why: After "in case", use the present simple for a future possibility, not "will".
When I was small, I would be afraid of dogs. Is "would be" right?

When I was small, I was afraid of dogs.
Why: "Would" describes repeated actions in the past. For a past feeling or state, use the simple past (or "used to be").
I use to walk to school when I was small. What is wrong?

I used to walk to school when I was small.
Why: The phrase for past habits is "used to", with a "d".
She is doing a MBA in Pune after working for two years. Is the article right?

She is doing an MBA in Pune after working for two years.
Why: The choice of "a" or "an" follows the sound. "MBA" starts with the sound "em", a vowel sound, so it takes "an".
Once upon time there lived a clever crow in a banyan tree. What is missing?

Once upon a time there lived a clever crow in a banyan tree.
Why: The fixed opening of a story is "once upon a time", with the article "a".
Every night I go to the bed at ten and wake up at six. Is "the bed" right?

Every night I go to bed at ten and wake up at six.
Why: "Go to bed" is a fixed phrase with no article when it means to sleep.
He studies hardly before exams, so he always does well. Is "hardly" the right word?

He studies hard before exams, so he always does well.
Why: "Hard" is both an adjective and an adverb. "Hardly" means "almost not", which changes the meaning.
She arrived lately at the station, and the train had gone. Which word is wrong?

She arrived late at the station, and the train had gone.
Why: "Late" is the adverb meaning "after the expected time". "Lately" means "recently".
The kite flew highly above the terrace and then dipped. Check the adverb.

The kite flew high above the terrace and then dipped.
Why: "High" is the adverb for height. "Highly" means "very much", as in "highly useful".
I am very tired to cook tonight. Can you fix the pattern?

I am too tired to cook tonight.
Why: Use "too + adjective + to + verb" to say that something stops an action. "Very" cannot be followed by "to + verb" in this way.
Because the road was closed, so we took another route. What is wrong?

Because the road was closed, we took another route.
Why: "Because" and "so" both show a cause, so use only one of them in the sentence.
I did not go to the park. Because I was tired. Is the second part a sentence?

I did not go to the park because I was tired.
Why: A "because" clause cannot normally stand alone as a sentence. Join it to the main clause.
A large amount of students joined the drama club this year. Which word is wrong?

A large number of students joined the drama club this year.
Why: Use "number" with countable nouns such as "students", and "amount" with uncountable ones such as "water".
The sweets were divided between the five children. Is "between" the right word?

The sweets were divided among the five children.
Why: "Among" is usually used for more than two people or things. "Between" suits two, or a few things seen as separate.
The programme starts at 6 pm in the evening. Is something repeated?

The programme starts at 6 pm.
Why: "Pm" already tells us it is the afternoon or evening, so "in the evening" repeats it.
Is very cold in the hills in December, so we pack warm clothes. What is missing?

It is very cold in the hills in December, so we pack warm clothes.
Why: An English sentence needs a subject. For weather, the subject is "it".
It has a small library in our village now. Is "it has" right?

There is a small library in our village now.
Why: To say that something exists, use "there is" or "there are". "It has" cannot do this job.
Please remember me to call Aunt Rita on Sunday. Is "remember me" right?

Please remind me to call Aunt Rita on Sunday.
Why: "Remind" means to help someone remember. "Remember" is what the person does for themselves.
I knew your sister at the fair yesterday. Is "knew" right for a first meeting?

I met your sister at the fair yesterday.
Why: "Know" describes a state of being familiar with someone. For a first meeting, use "met" (or "got to know").
She paid the tickets by card at the counter. Is something missing?

She paid for the tickets by card at the counter.
Why: "Pay" takes the person or the amount directly. For the thing you buy, use "pay for".
She is putting a green saree today and looks lovely. Is "putting" the right verb?

She is wearing a green saree today and looks lovely.
Why: "Wear" describes what you have on. "Put on" is the action of dressing.
My sister participated to the quiz and came second. Which preposition is right?

My sister participated in the quiz and came second.
Why: The usual phrase is "participate in".
She cannot concentrate in her work when the music is loud. Which preposition is right?

She cannot concentrate on her work when the music is loud.
Why: "Concentrate" is followed by "on".
I am not sure whether she will come or no. How do I fix the end?

I am not sure whether she will come or not.
Why: The fixed pair is "whether ... or not".
Almost people in our street keep a pet. Which word is wrong?

Most people in our street keep a pet.
Why: "Most" works before a noun. "Almost" is an adverb, so it needs "all" or "every": "almost all people".
How about to visit the museum on Saturday? Is "how about to" right?

How about visiting the museum on Saturday?
Why: "How about" is followed by an -ing form.
No sooner did he sit down when the bell rang. Something is wrong with the pair of words.

No sooner did he sit down than the bell rang.
Why: "No sooner" is paired with "than", not "when".
Do you have a time to talk about the schedule? What is off?

Do you have time to talk about the schedule?
Why: When it means free time, "time" is uncountable, so it takes no "a".
I am sorry for late, the bus broke down on the way. Please correct.

I am sorry for being late. The bus broke down on the way.
Why: After "sorry for", use a noun or an -ing form, so "being late". "Sorry for late" is heard in Indian English. A comma should not join two full sentences.
Thank you for your helping me with the project. Is "your helping" right?

Thank you for helping me with the project.
Why: "Thank you for" is followed by an -ing form or a noun ("for your help"), not both. "Your helping" is correct only in very formal writing.
Do you know to swim? How do I ask this properly?

Do you know how to swim?
Why: For a skill, "know" needs "how" before "to + verb". You could also ask "Can you swim?".
See you on tomorrow at the bus stop. Is "on" needed?

See you tomorrow at the bus stop.
Why: "Tomorrow" is an adverb of time and takes no preposition. "On tomorrow" is heard in Indian English.
I admire her patient with young children. Which word should change?

I admire her patience with young children.
Why: After "her", a noun is needed. "Patient" is the adjective; the noun is "patience".
What is the different between a lake and a pond? Is the word right?

What is the difference between a lake and a pond?
Why: "The" needs a noun after it. "Different" is the adjective; the noun is "difference".
Please keep the door close so the cat cannot get out. Which word is wrong?

Please keep the door closed so the cat cannot get out.
Why: To describe the state of the door, use the participle "closed". "Close" would be the verb, or the adjective meaning "near".
How long is your school from here? Is "how long" right?

How far is your school from here?
Why: "How far" asks about distance. "How long" asks about time or length.
I'm going to the market; do you need anything? Can I use a semicolon here?

It is acceptable.
Why: A semicolon can join two closely linked sentences, though a full stop after "market" is just as good. A comma alone would be a comma splice.
I shall be happy to help you with the form. Is "shall" too old-fashioned?

It is correct, and it sounds polite.
Why: "Shall" with "I" or "we" is correct in offers and formal writing. "Will" is more common today, and both are fine.
