Anyone who wants a seat should raise their hand. Should it be "his or her" instead of "their"?

Both are acceptable, so no change is needed.
Why: Singular "they" and "their" for someone of unknown gender are widely accepted today. "His or her" is more formal.
There is some bread and two eggs on the plate. Should it be "are" because of the eggs?

No, "is" is acceptable here.
Why: After "there", the verb usually agrees with the first item in the list, "some bread". "Are" is also common in speech.
Had I known about the delay, I would have left earlier. Is it okay to start with "Had I known"?

Yes, it is correct.
Why: "Had I known" is a formal way to say "If I had known", with the same third-conditional meaning.
I look forward to seeing you next week. Should it be "to see"?

No, "seeing" is right.
Why: In "look forward to", the "to" is a preposition, so the verb after it ends in -ing.
If I were you, I would apologise to her. Is "were" correct with "I"?

Yes, "were" is correct here.
Why: In an unreal condition, formal English uses "were" for all subjects. "Was" is common in speech.
Mum and Dad are coming to my school's Annual Day. Do "Mum" and "Dad" need capitals here?

Yes, the capitals are correct.
Why: Family words take a capital when they are used as names, as in "Mum and Dad". After "my" they stay lowercase.
The Himalayas is the highest mountain range in the world. Is the verb okay?

The Himalayas are the highest mountain range in the world.
Why: "Himalayas" is a plural name, so it takes the plural verb "are".
I have met your cousin two years ago at Neha's wedding. Which tense should I use?

I met your cousin two years ago at Neha's wedding.
Why: With a finished time such as "two years ago", English uses the past simple, not the present perfect.
I am very exciting about the science fair next week. Can you correct it?

I am very excited about the science fair next week.
Why: "Excited" describes how a person feels; "exciting" describes the thing that causes the feeling.
My brother didn't came home for lunch today. What is the mistake?

My brother didn't come home for lunch today.
Why: After "didn't" the main verb stays in its base form ("come"), because "didn't" already shows the past.
Do you can play the flute? Please fix my question.

Can you play the flute?
Why: "Can" is a modal verb, so it makes questions by moving before the subject, without "do".
This steel tiffin box belongs for my grandfather. Which word is wrong?

This steel tiffin box belongs to my grandfather.
Why: The verb "belong" is followed by "to" when you name the owner.
I like to listen the radio while I cook dinner. Please correct this.

I like to listen to the radio while I cook dinner.
Why: "Listen" needs "to" before the thing you listen to.
My neighbour has been suffering with fever for three days now. Is "with" okay?

My neighbour has been suffering from fever for three days now.
Why: "Suffer" is normally followed by "from" when you name the problem.
She applied to the receptionist job at the clinic last week. Fix the preposition.

She applied for the receptionist job at the clinic last week.
Why: You apply "for" a job, and "to" a company or a person.
My grandmother believes on the power of prayer. Please check.

My grandmother believes in the power of prayer.
Why: "Believe in" is the usual pattern when you trust that something is real or valuable.
The guard was accused for stealing a bicycle, but he was innocent. What should it be?

The guard was accused of stealing a bicycle, but he was innocent.
Why: "Accuse" is followed by "of" and the act: "accused of stealing".
I thank to you for helping me with the luggage. Is this right?

I thank you for helping me with the luggage.
Why: "Thank" takes the person directly, without "to", and "for" then gives the reason.
She has lack of confidence in maths, but she is improving. Is something missing?

She has a lack of confidence in maths, but she is improving.
Why: The noun "lack" is used as "a lack of", so it needs "a" before it.
My shirt is same like yours, but mine is bigger. Please correct it.

My shirt is the same as yours, but mine is bigger.
Why: "The same" is followed by "as", not "like", and it needs "the" before it.
The new bypass is more better than the old road. Fix this, please.

The new bypass is better than the old road.
Why: "Better" is already a comparative form, so "more" is not added.
Today's heat is much more worse than yesterday's. What is wrong?

Today's heat is much worse than yesterday's.
Why: "Worse" is already a comparative form, so "more" is not needed. "Much" can stay to add strength.
This brand of cotton is superior than that one. Is "than" right?

This brand of cotton is superior to that one.
Why: "Superior" is followed by "to", not "than". The same is true of "inferior".
Let's look the cricket final at my house tonight. Which verb is better?

Let's watch the cricket final at my house tonight.
Why: "Look" needs "at" and means to turn your eyes towards something; for a match or a show, use "watch".
I am liking this song very much. Can you simplify the verb?

I like this song very much.
Why: "Like" is a state verb, and state verbs of feeling are not usually used in the continuous form.
Rarely he eats food from outside. Is the order right?

Rarely does he eat food from outside.
Why: When a negative-sounding adverb such as "rarely" starts the sentence, the helping verb "does" comes before the subject and the main verb goes back to "eat".
Which one you want, the red pen or the blue pen? Please fix the question.

Which one do you want, the red pen or the blue pen?
Why: A question needs the helping verb "do" before the subject "you".
My mother sang all the day while she cleaned the house. Is "the" needed?

My mother sang all day while she cleaned the house.
Why: The set phrase is "all day", with no "the".
None of the boys have finished the quiz yet. Is "have" okay with "none"?

This is acceptable as written.
Why: "None" can take a singular or a plural verb. "Have" is very common in everyday English, and "has" is the stricter formal choice.
I like to eat the fruits in the morning. Is "the" needed?

I like to eat fruits in the morning.
Why: When you talk about a kind of food in general, you use no article.
We saw a peacock who was dancing near the pond. Is "who" right for a bird?

We saw a peacock that was dancing near the pond.
Why: "That" or "which" is usually used for animals. "Who" is kept for people, and sometimes for a pet that is treated like a person.
Feed your pet regular, and it will stay happy. What is the right word?

Feed your pet regularly, and it will stay happy.
Why: The word describes how you feed, so it must be an adverb ("regularly"), not the adjective "regular".
We exchanged sweets and good wishes with our neighbours at Diwali. Is this correct?

No change needed.
Why: The past simple suits a finished event, "at" is the usual preposition for a festival, and "exchange ... with" is the right pattern.
I am worried for my sister's result. What should the preposition be?

I am worried about my sister's result.
Why: "Worried" is usually followed by "about" when it names the thing that troubles you.
I read the novel twice and then I lend it to my friend. Please check the verb.

I read the novel twice and then I lent it to my friend.
Why: The story is in the past, and the past tense of "lend" is "lent".
The metro in our city is very clean and quick, and it saves a lot of times. Fix please.

The metro in our city is very clean and quick, and it saves a lot of time.
Why: In this meaning "time" is uncountable, so it has no plural form.
We went to a trip to Munnar last December. Which word is wrong?

We went on a trip to Munnar last December.
Why: The usual phrase is "go on a trip".
The train from Chennai will arrive on 6:30 in the evening. Please correct.

The train from Chennai will arrive at 6:30 in the evening.
Why: Use "at" with a clock time.
Please take care about your bag in the crowd. Fix the phrase.

Please take care of your bag in the crowd.
Why: The phrase is "take care of" something or someone.
Kindly do the needful and send the form by tomorrow. Is "do the needful" correct?

It is fine in Indian English as written.
Why: "Do the needful" is a well-known phrase in Indian business English, but it can sound dated elsewhere, so in a message to readers abroad you may prefer "please send the form by tomorrow".
After exercise, I feel more energetic and relax. Please fix the last word.

After exercise, I feel more energetic and relaxed.
Why: After "feel" you need adjectives, and "relax" is a verb. The adjective is "relaxed", which matches "energetic".
My grandfather has gone for a checkup, and he will back soon. What is missing?

My grandfather has gone for a checkup, and he will be back soon.
Why: "Will" needs a verb after it, and "back" is not one, so "be" is missing.
I owe my cousin two hundred rupees, and I will pay him back on Saturday. Anything to fix?

No, it is already correct.
Why: "Owe" takes the person and the amount, "pay him back" is the normal phrasal verb, and "on Saturday" is the right preposition.
The school fees was increased this year. What is wrong?

The school fees were increased this year.
Why: "Fees" is a plural noun, so it takes the plural verb "were".
Tanvi ran so fast that she beat all the other runners and win the race. Fix the last verb.

Tanvi ran so fast that she beat all the other runners and won the race.
Why: The story is in the past, so the verb after "and" must also be past: "won".
She catched the ball with one hand and the crowd cheered. What is the right form?

She caught the ball with one hand and the crowd cheered.
Why: "Catch" is irregular, and its past form is "caught".
I might can join the chess club next month. Is this okay?

I might be able to join the chess club next month.
Why: Two modal verbs cannot be used together, so "be able to" replaces "can" after "might".
We climbed up the hill till the top and sat under a tree. Is "till" right?

We climbed up the hill to the top and sat under a tree.
Why: "Till" is mainly used for time; for a place, "to" is the usual word, although "till" for place is heard in Indian English.
Our dog is very friendly with stranger and loves children. What is wrong?

Our dog is very friendly with strangers and loves children.
Why: "Stranger" is a countable noun; speaking about people in general, it needs the plural "strangers".
The video was so long that I felt asleep halfway. Which word is wrong?

The video was so long that I fell asleep halfway.
Why: The phrase is "fall asleep", and its past tense is "fell". "Felt" is the past of "feel".
Is the Wi-Fi working? I can't connect to it. Can you check this short message?

Yes, that's right as it stands.
Why: Both sentences are complete and correct, and "connect to" is the right pattern.
I was late to school because the bus got stuck in traffic. Please correct it.

I was late for school because the bus got stuck in traffic.
Why: The usual phrase is "late for" a place or an event.
There is a pharmacy, a bakery, and a post office on this street. Is the list punctuated right?

This is already correct.
Why: The comma before "and" in a list is optional; some writers use it and some leave it out, so both styles are fine.
The artist mixed blue and yellow to make a green. Is "a" needed?

The artist mixed blue and yellow to make green.
Why: When a colour is named as a thing in general, no article is used.
The museum has a lots of old paintings and statues. What should I change?

The museum has a lot of old paintings and statues.
Why: "A lot of" is the correct form; "lots of" is also fine but takes no "a".
Wash your hands before to eat. What is wrong with this?

Wash your hands before eating.
Why: After the preposition "before" the verb takes the -ing form.
The boy who won the race, got a medal from the chief guest. Is the comma needed?

The boy who won the race got a medal from the chief guest.
Why: A comma should not separate the subject ("The boy who won the race") from its verb ("got").
i think i left my geometry box in the classroom. What should I fix?

I think I left my geometry box in the classroom.
Why: The pronoun "I" is always written as a capital letter, and so is the first word of a sentence.
My cousin speaks english and hindi, and she is learning tamil. Please check the capitals.

My cousin speaks English and Hindi, and she is learning Tamil.
Why: The names of languages are proper nouns, so they begin with a capital letter.
Cut the apple into two halfs and share it with your sister. Is "halfs" right?

Cut the apple into two halves and share it with your sister.
Why: Nouns like "half" change the -f to -ves in the plural.
Cats are said to have nine lifes. Please check the plural.

Cats are said to have nine lives.
Why: The plural of "life" is "lives", with -f changing to -ves.
My foots are cold when I walk on the wet grass. What is wrong?

My feet are cold when I walk on the wet grass.
Why: "Foot" has an irregular plural, "feet".
Two thiefs were caught near the station last night. Is the plural correct?

Two thieves were caught near the station last night.
Why: "Thief" changes to "thieves" in the plural.
I washed my cloths and hung them on the balcony. Is that the right word?

I washed my clothes and hung them on the balcony.
Why: "Cloths" are pieces of fabric, such as dusters; the things you wear are "clothes".
Lightening flashed across the sky, and then the thunder rolled. Check the first word.

Lightning flashed across the sky, and then the thunder rolled.
Why: The flash in the sky is "lightning". "Lightening" means making something lighter.
She bought her lunch from home in a steel box. Which verb is right?

She brought her lunch from home in a steel box.
Why: "Bring" means to carry something along, and its past form is "brought". "Bought" is the past of "buy".
We practise to play carrom every evening, so we are getting better. Fix the verb form.

We practise playing carrom every evening, so we are getting better.
Why: After "practise" the next verb takes the -ing form.
My sister has finished to eat her lunch already. What is wrong?

My sister has finished eating her lunch already.
Why: "Finish" is followed by the -ing form, not "to" plus a verb.
I hope to seeing you at the reunion in December. Please correct.

I hope to see you at the reunion in December.
Why: "Hope to" is followed by the base form of the verb.
Try to avoid to take the main road at five o'clock because of the traffic. Fix the verb.

Try to avoid taking the main road at five o'clock because of the traffic.
Why: "Avoid" is followed by the -ing form.
I left early so that I can catch the first bus. Is "can" okay?

I left early so that I could catch the first bus.
Why: The sentence is about the past, so "can" changes to "could" after "so that".
Our teacher asked us to not talk during the test. Is "to not talk" wrong?

It is acceptable as written.
Why: Many careful writers prefer "not to talk", but "to not talk" is widely used and understood, so nothing needs correcting.
My manager told me coming early on Monday. What is wrong?

My manager told me to come early on Monday.
Why: "Tell" plus a person is followed by "to" and the base form of the verb.
The neighbours' dog barked all night, so nobody could sleep well. Is the apostrophe right?

Yes, the apostrophe is in the right place.
Why: The neighbours are more than one person, so the apostrophe comes after the plural "s" ("neighbours'").
Meera very good at chess, and she teaching me the openings. Please check the verbs.

Meera is very good at chess, and she is teaching me the openings.
Why: The verb "is" is missing twice: once before the adjective "good", and once before "teaching".
I want go to the market with you after school. What is missing?

I want to go to the market with you after school.
Why: "Want" is followed by "to" and the base form of the verb.
It was so windy yesterday that the kites flied very high. Is "flied" right?

It was so windy yesterday that the kites flew very high.
Why: "Fly" is irregular, and its past form is "flew".
The mango tree growed taller every year. Please fix the verb.

The mango tree grew taller every year.
Why: The past tense of "grow" is "grew".
At Eid, we wear new clothes and visit to our relatives. Which word is extra?

At Eid, we wear new clothes and visit our relatives.
Why: "Visit" takes its object directly, so no "to" is needed.
The festival of lights is marked by lighting lamps, bursting crackers and exchange sweets. Check the list.

The festival of lights is marked by lighting lamps, bursting crackers and exchanging sweets.
Why: The items in a list after "by" should have the same form, so "exchange" becomes "exchanging".
Lakshmi borrowed three books from the library, but she has returned only two of them. Does this sound natural?

Yes, it sounds natural.
Why: The present perfect "has returned" links the earlier borrowing with the situation now, and "only" is placed right before "two of them".
We must save our money for rainy day. Is something missing?

We must save our money for a rainy day.
Why: The idiom is "for a rainy day", with the article "a".
Which is right, "sorry for" or "sorry about", in this line? I am sorry for being late yesterday.

Both are correct here, so your sentence needs no change.
Why: "Sorry for" and "sorry about" can both be followed by an -ing phrase; "sorry for" is a little more common when you apologise.
The mall is crowded in weekends, so we go on weekdays. Fix the preposition.

The mall is crowded on weekends, so we go on weekdays.
Why: Use "on weekends" in American English or "at weekends" in British English, not "in".
Is there a good resturant near the bus stand? Check my spelling.

Is there a good restaurant near the bus stand?
Why: The word is spelled "restaurant", with "au" in the last part.
The teacher announced the results on Febuary the first. Spelling, please.

The teacher announced the results on February the first.
Why: "February" has an "r" after the "b": Feb-ru-ary.
My favourite subject is mathmatics. Is it spelled right?

My favourite subject is mathematics.
Why: The word has the letters "hem" in the middle: "mathematics".
The temperture dropped sharply after the rain. What is wrong?

The temperature dropped sharply after the rain.
Why: The word is spelled "temperature", with "era" in the middle.
This chair is very comfortible, so I sit here to study. Which word is misspelled?

This chair is very comfortable, so I sit here to study.
Why: The word ends in "-able": "comfortable".
I bought some vegitables and a packet of paneer from the market. Check the spelling.

I bought some vegetables and a packet of paneer from the market.
Why: The word is "vegetables", with "e" after the "g".
I beleive our class will win the quiz this year. Spelling, please.

I believe our class will win the quiz this year.
Why: In "believe" the letters go "ie", as in "field" and "piece".
She has an unusual talent, and she acheived a lot at a young age. Please check the spelling.

She has an unusual talent, and she achieved a lot at a young age.
Why: The spelling is "achieved", with "ie" after the "ch".
Our neibour showed us photos of his trip to a foriegn country. Two spellings look wrong.

Our neighbour showed us photos of his trip to a foreign country.
Why: "Neighbour" is spelled with "eigh", and "foreign" is an exception that has "ei".
Our exam is on the twelth of March. Is that spelled right?

Our exam is on the twelfth of March.
Why: The number is "twelve" plus "th", so the "f" stays: "twelfth".
My uncle has been working at the bank for fourty years. Is "fourty" spelled right?

My uncle has been working at the bank for forty years.
Why: "Forty" has no "u", although "four" and "fourteen" do.
The team will go to the finals on the forth of May. Which word is wrong?

The team will go to the finals on the fourth of May.
Why: The ordinal number is "fourth", and "forth" is a different word meaning "forward".
Our flat is on the second storey of the building. Is "storey" a mistake?

No, it is not a mistake.
Why: "Storey" is the British spelling for a floor of a building, and "story" is the American one, so either is correct in its variety.
I need to by a new notebook before school starts. Please check the word.

I need to buy a new notebook before school starts.
Why: "Buy" means to pay for something; "by" is a preposition.
A rainbow appears when sunlight pass through raindrops. What should the verb be?

A rainbow appears when sunlight passes through raindrops.
Why: "Sunlight" is a singular subject, so the present-tense verb takes -s.
Carrom is a game who needs a steady hand. Is "who" right?

Carrom is a game that needs a steady hand.
Why: "Who" is used for people; for a thing such as a game, use "that" or "which".
Can I play too? Said the little boy. Please fix the punctuation.

"Can I play too?" said the little boy.
Why: Spoken words go inside quotation marks, and "said" starts with a small letter because it continues the same sentence.
My aunt is wearing a beautiful silk saree and a gold earrings. Please fix this.

My aunt is wearing a beautiful silk saree and gold earrings.
Why: "Earrings" is plural, so it cannot take "a".
My new shoes are too tight for me, so I will exchange it tomorrow. What is wrong?

My new shoes are too tight for me, so I will exchange them tomorrow.
Why: "Shoes" is plural, so the pronoun that refers to it must be "them".
Don't take tension about the exam; just do your best. Is "take tension" okay?

Don't worry about the exam; just do your best.
Why: "Take tension" is common in Indian English, but "worry" or "stress" is the usual wording in other varieties, so "worry" is the safer choice.
It took us three hours reaching Mysore by road. Please correct.

It took us three hours to reach Mysore by road.
Why: After "It took us" plus a time, the next verb takes "to" and the base form.
I like all kinds of music except of rock. What should I change?

I like all kinds of music except rock.
Why: "Except" is followed directly by the thing left out, so "of" is not needed.
It is a ten minutes walk from our school to the lake. Is the plural right?

It is a ten-minute walk from our school to the lake.
Why: When a number and a unit work together as an adjective before a noun, they are joined by a hyphen and the unit stays singular.
Fifty percents of the class passed with distinction. What is wrong?

Fifty percent of the class passed with distinction.
Why: "Percent" does not take a plural -s, even after numbers above one.
My aunt has ten years' experience as a nurse. Does "years" need an apostrophe?

Yes, the apostrophe is needed and correctly placed.
Why: "Ten years' experience" is a plural possessive, like "two weeks' notice", so the apostrophe follows the "s".
The customer was not satisfied of the service in the shop. Which word is wrong?

The customer was not satisfied with the service in the shop.
Why: "Satisfied" is followed by "with", not "of".
My little brother is crazy for cricket and plays every day. Please check the preposition.

My little brother is crazy about cricket and plays every day.
Why: "Crazy about" is the usual phrase for a strong liking.
Can you imagine to live without a phone for a whole week? Fix the verb.

Can you imagine living without a phone for a whole week?
Why: "Imagine" is followed by the -ing form.
We have two cats. One is white and another is black. What should I change?

We have two cats. One is white and the other is black.
Why: When there are only two, you say "one ... the other"; "another" means one more out of several.
Can I have another two biscuits, please? Is "another two" okay, or should it be "two more"?

Both are correct, so your sentence needs no change.
Why: "Another" can come before a number, as in "another two biscuits", and it means the same as "two more".
The instructions on this form are very confused, so I need help. Which word is wrong?

The instructions on this form are very confusing, so I need help.
Why: "Confusing" describes the thing that causes the confusion; "confused" describes the person who feels it.
He gave a good speach at the farewell party. Check the spelling.

He gave a good speech at the farewell party.
Why: The noun is spelled "speech", with "ee".
I ate a sandwhich and drank a glass of milk before the match. Is the spelling right?

I ate a sandwich and drank a glass of milk before the match.
Why: "Sandwich" has no "h" after the "w".
Unfortunatly, I could not come to your birthday. Check the first word.

Unfortunately, I could not come to your birthday.
Why: The adverb is "unfortunately", made from "unfortunate" plus "-ly", so the "e" stays.
I leave with my grandparents near the temple. Which word is wrong?

I live with my grandparents near the temple.
Why: "Live" means to have your home somewhere. "Leave" means to go away from a place.
We took a boat on the river ganga at sunrise. Does "ganga" need a capital?

We took a boat on the river Ganga at sunrise.
Why: The name of a river begins with a capital letter. "River" itself may be written with a small or a capital letter, depending on the style.
We learn new vocabularies every week in English class. Is "vocabularies" a word?

We learn new vocabulary every week in English class.
Why: "Vocabularies" does exist, but only for separate word lists; for the words a person learns, "vocabulary" is normally used without an -s.
I packed all my stuffs in one small bag. Is "stuffs" right?

I packed all my stuff in one small bag.
Why: "Stuff" is uncountable, so it has no plural form.
That bicycle is not my; it is hers. What should the pronoun be?

That bicycle is not mine; it is hers.
Why: When no noun follows, the possessive pronoun "mine" is used instead of "my".
I am looking after my keys; have you seen them? Is "looking after" right?

I am looking for my keys; have you seen them?
Why: "Look for" means to search for something. "Look after" means to take care of.
We ran out sugar, so I went to the shop. What is missing?

We ran out of sugar, so I went to the shop.
Why: The phrasal verb "run out" needs "of" before the thing that is finished.
I found out some old photographs in a box under the bed. Is "found out" right?

I found some old photographs in a box under the bed.
Why: "Find" means to come across something; "find out" means to learn a fact.
It was a blessing in the disguise that the match was cancelled. Check the idiom.

It was a blessing in disguise that the match was cancelled.
Why: The idiom is "a blessing in disguise", with no "the".
You hit the nail in the head with that idea. Is the idiom right?

You hit the nail on the head with that idea.
Why: The idiom is "hit the nail on the head", meaning to describe something exactly.
She felt under the weather this morning, so she stayed home. Have I used the idiom correctly?

Yes, you have used it correctly.
Why: "Under the weather" means slightly unwell, and your sentence uses it naturally with the past tense.
My cousin stays in Pune with his parents. Is "stays" right for where he lives?

It is fine in Indian English as it is.
Why: In India "stay" is an everyday word for "live"; in British or American English it more often means a short visit, so "lives" is clearer for readers there.
My father is out of station until Friday. Is this correct English?

This works as written in Indian English.
Why: "Out of station" is a common Indian English phrase for being away from the city; in other varieties "out of town" is more usual.
I like also the rainy season, but not the floods. Is the order right?

I also like the rainy season, but not the floods.
Why: "Also" normally goes before the main verb, not after it.
My uncle walks daily for half hour near the lake. What is missing?

My uncle walks daily for half an hour near the lake.
Why: The usual phrase is "half an hour", with "an" before "hour".
Mr Das teaches music in our school, and he has the beautiful voice. Which article is wrong?

Mr Das teaches music in our school, and he has a beautiful voice.
Why: The voice is mentioned for the first time and is not one specific known thing, so it takes "a".
Our neighbours move to Chennai last month, and we miss them a lot. Fix the verb.

Our neighbours moved to Chennai last month, and we miss them a lot.
Why: "Last month" is a finished time, so the verb must be in the past simple.
I tried this board game for first time yesterday, and I loved it. What is missing?

I tried this board game for the first time yesterday, and I loved it.
Why: "For the first time" is a fixed phrase that needs "the".
Our club meets every Saturdays at the community hall. Is the plural right?

Our club meets every Saturday at the community hall.
Why: After "every" the noun stays singular.
The old king was ruled for many years and everyone loved him. Is "was ruled" okay?

The old king ruled for many years and everyone loved him.
Why: Here the king is the one who rules, so the verb is active, "ruled". "Was ruled" would mean that someone else ruled him.
The fort was built on the sixteenth century by a local chief. Which word is wrong?

The fort was built in the sixteenth century by a local chief.
Why: Use "in" with centuries, years and months.
Our history teacher told us that India become independent in 1947. Fix the verb.

Our history teacher told us that India became independent in 1947.
Why: The event is in the past, so "become" must be the past form "became".
I borrowed three books from library and returned them on time. What is missing?

I borrowed three books from the library and returned them on time.
Why: A particular, known place such as "the library" needs "the".
You cannot take the reference books at home. Is "at home" right?

You cannot take the reference books home.
Why: "Home" is an adverb here, so it follows "take" directly without a preposition.
It seems like it's going to rain; I can feel in the air. What is missing at the end?

It seems like it's going to rain; I can feel it in the air.
Why: "Feel" needs an object, so the pronoun "it" is missing.
My nephew is very talent in drawing. Which word should change?

My nephew is very talented in drawing.
Why: After "very" you need an adjective, and the adjective form of "talent" is "talented".
Boil the milk and let it cools down. What is wrong with the last verb?

Boil the milk and let it cool down.
Why: After "let" plus an object the verb stays in the base form.
We gave Nina a card and wish her a happy birthday. Please check the tense.

We gave Nina a card and wished her a happy birthday.
Why: Both actions happened in the past, so the second verb must also be past: "wished".
The tailor gave me a discount of ten percent in this shirt. Which preposition is wrong?

The shopkeeper gave me a discount of ten percent on this shirt.
Why: A discount is given "on" the item.
My father goes to work by foot every morning. Is "by foot" right?

My father goes to work on foot every morning.
Why: The fixed phrase is "on foot", while "by" is used with vehicles such as bus or train.
The bus conductor asked me to get off from the bus at the next stop. Is "from" needed?

The bus conductor asked me to get off the bus at the next stop.
Why: "Get off" takes its object directly, so "from" is not needed.
The train is arriving in platform number three. Which word is wrong?

The train is arriving on platform number three.
Why: We say "on a platform" because the platform is a surface to stand on.
Please fill this form in capital letter and sign on the bottom. Two things need fixing.

Please fill this form in capital letters and sign at the bottom.
Why: "Capital letters" is plural because there are many letters, and "at the bottom" is the usual phrase for a position on a page.
He asked for a permission to leave early today. What should I change?

He asked for permission to leave early today.
Why: "Permission" is uncountable, so it cannot take "a".
Thanks for the notes, I really appreciate. Is something missing?

Thanks for the notes, I really appreciate it.
Why: "Appreciate" needs an object, so "it" is missing.
I am looking forward for the holidays. Which word is wrong?

I am looking forward to the holidays.
Why: The phrase is "look forward to", where "to" is a preposition.
A group of lions are called a pride. Is the verb right?

A group of lions is called a pride.
Why: The subject is "a group", which is singular, so the verb is "is".
Whales are not fishes; they are mammals. Is "fishes" okay?

Whales are not fish; they are mammals.
Why: "Fish" is the usual plural. "Fishes" is used mainly when talking about different kinds of fish.
The team are celebrating their win with sweets. Should it be "is" or "are" after "team"?

Your sentence is fine as it is.
Why: British English often treats a team as plural, as you did with "are" and "their"; American English prefers "is" and "its".
The data shows that the lake is shrinking every year. Is "data shows" okay, or should it be "data show"?

Both are used, so your sentence stands.
Why: "Data" is treated as singular in everyday English, and as plural ("data show") in formal scientific writing.
I would like to try on this jacket, please. Is "try on" in the right place?

Yes, it is in the right place.
Why: With a noun such as "this jacket" the particle can come before or after it; with a pronoun it must come in the middle ("try it on").
It has been raining since yesterday evening, so the match was postponed. Please check my tenses.

The tenses are right, so nothing needs to change.
Why: "Has been raining" with "since" fits rain that is still going on, and the past simple "was postponed" fits a decision already made.
Despite he was tired, he finished the race. Please fix it.

Although he was tired, he finished the race.
Why: "Despite" is followed by a noun or an -ing form; before a full clause with its own subject and verb, use "although".
During I was cooking, the power went off. What is wrong?

While I was cooking, the power went off.
Why: "During" is followed by a noun ("during dinner"); before a clause, use "while".
I have been never to the Amber Fort, but I want to go. Fix the word order.

I have never been to the Amber Fort, but I want to go.
Why: "Never" goes between the helping verb "have" and the main verb "been".
Meena gained the first prize in the painting contest. Is "gained" right?

Meena won the first prize in the painting contest.
Why: You "win" a prize or a race; "gain" is used for things such as weight, skills or experience.
Please seat down; the film is about to start. What should the verb be?

Please sit down; the film is about to start.
Why: "Sit down" is what you do to take a seat; "seat" needs an object, as in "seat the guests".
He dressed a blue shirt and a black cap for the match. Which verb is right?

He wore a blue shirt and a black cap for the match.
Why: "Wear" means to have clothes on; "dress" is used for putting clothes on a person ("dress the baby") or in "dressed in".
Red colour fits me well, so I bought this kurta. Is "fits" the right verb?

Red colour suits me well, so I bought this kurta.
Why: "Suit" is used when a colour or style looks good on you, while "fit" is about size and shape.
The price of tomatoes is very cheap this week. Is "cheap" right for a price?

The price of tomatoes is very low this week.
Why: A price is high or low, while the things we buy are cheap or expensive.
Our basketball captain is very high for his age. Which word is wrong?

Our basketball captain is very tall for his age.
Why: "Tall" describes people; "high" is used for things and places far above the ground.
Can you recomend a good mystery for the holidays? Spelling, please.

Can you recommend a good mystery for the holidays?
Why: The word is spelled with one "c" and a double "m": re-com-mend.
Her pronounciation of English words is very clear. Is it spelled right?

Her pronunciation of English words is very clear.
Why: The noun "pronunciation" drops the "o" that is in the verb "pronounce".
Our shop has a big sail on school bags this Sunday. Which word is wrong?

Our shop has a big sale on school bags this Sunday.
Why: A "sale" is when goods are sold at lower prices; a "sail" is the cloth on a boat.
She played an important roll in the street play. Is "roll" right?

She played an important role in the street play.
Why: A "role" is the part a person plays; "roll" is something that turns or a kind of bread.
I wood like a cup of tea, please. Check the spelling.

I would like a cup of tea, please.
Why: "Would" is the helping verb used in polite requests; "wood" comes from trees.
I go for a walk at evening with my grandmother. Is "at evening" right?

I go for a walk in the evening with my grandmother.
Why: Use "in the" with parts of the day such as morning, afternoon and evening; "at night" is the exception.
Independence Day is celebrated in 15 August every year. Which word is wrong?

Independence Day is celebrated on 15 August every year.
Why: Use "on" with exact dates and days.
People throw garbages on the road, and the street gets dirty. Is "garbages" right?

People throw garbage on the road, and the street gets dirty.
Why: "Garbage" is uncountable and normally has no plural.
The storm caused heavy damages to the crops in our village. Is "damages" right?

The storm caused heavy damage to the crops in our village.
Why: In this meaning "damage" is uncountable; "damages" is used only in the legal sense of money paid as compensation.
Please come at five thirty o'clock tomorrow. Is "o'clock" right?

Please come at five thirty tomorrow.
Why: "O'clock" is used only for whole hours, as in "five o'clock", not for times with minutes.
Would you like anything other with your tea? Fix the phrase.

Would you like anything else with your tea?
Why: After "anything", the word "else" means something more.
I would rather go by bus than to walk in this heat. What is wrong?

I would rather go by bus than walk in this heat.
Why: After "would rather" and the matching "than", the verb is in the base form without "to".
We hired a small flat near the station last year. Is "hired" right?

We rented a small flat near the station last year.
Why: You usually "rent" a flat; "hire" is used for people, or for vehicles and equipment for a short time.
My mother is a very good cooker, and everyone loves her biryani. Which word is wrong?

My mother is a very good cook, and everyone loves her biryani.
Why: A person who cooks is a "cook"; a "cooker" is the stove or appliance.
The picnic was very funny, and we want to go again. Is "funny" the right word?

The picnic was great fun, and we want to go again.
Why: "Fun" means enjoyable, while "funny" means that something made you laugh, so "fun" suits a day you enjoyed.
She drew the sketch by a pencil. Which preposition is wrong?

She drew the sketch with a pencil.
Why: Use "with" for the tool you use.
What of these two bags is yours? Fix the first word.

Which of these two bags is yours?
Why: "Which" is used to choose from a small, known set.
I feel myself very tired after the long journey. Is "myself" needed?

I feel very tired after the long journey.
Why: After "feel" an adjective follows directly, so "myself" is not needed here.
Let's don't waste time; the bus leaves soon. What should it be?

Let's not waste time; the bus leaves soon.
Why: The negative of "let's" is "let's not".
Why not we go by train today? Please fix the question.

Why don't we go by train today?
Why: "Why don't we" is the usual way to suggest something with a subject; "why not" is followed by a verb alone, as in "Why not go by train?".
We went yesterday to the market and bought vegetables. Is the word order right?

We went to the market yesterday and bought vegetables.
Why: In an English sentence the place usually comes before the time.
I go always to the temple on Mondays. Please fix the word order.

I always go to the temple on Mondays.
Why: A frequency adverb such as "always" goes before the main verb.
My cousin doesn't has a bicycle, so he walks to the lake. What is wrong?

My cousin doesn't have a bicycle, so he walks to the lake.
Why: After "doesn't" the verb is in the base form, "have".
My uncle bought a watch to me on my birthday. Which word is wrong?

My uncle bought a watch for me on my birthday.
Why: "Buy" takes "for" with the person who gets the thing.
I will tell you the story latter. Is "latter" right?

I will tell you the story later.
Why: "Later" means after some time; "latter" means the second of two things already named.
She cried at the lose of her pet parrot. Which word is wrong?

She cried at the loss of her pet parrot.
Why: The noun is "loss", with a double "s"; "lose" is the verb.
I practice the violin every evening for an hour. Is "practice" right as a verb?

It is right in American English.
Why: American English spells both the noun and the verb "practice", while British English writes the verb as "practise" and keeps "practice" for the noun.
My father was borned in a small village near Madurai. What is wrong?

My father was born in a small village near Madurai.
Why: "Was born" uses the form "born"; "borned" is not a word.
Can my sister join the game aswell? Check the spelling.

Can my sister join the game as well?
Why: "As well" is written as two words.
Please sent me the file by evening. Fix the verb.

Please send me the file by evening.
Why: An instruction after "please" uses the base form "send"; "sent" is the past form.
My phone keeps hanging, so I will restart it. Is "hanging" right?

My phone keeps freezing, so I will restart it.
Why: "Hanging" for a stuck screen is common in Indian English, but "freezing" is understood everywhere.
I have saved the file in my computer. Which preposition is right?

I have saved the file on my computer.
Why: Files are usually saved "on" a computer, phone or disk, and "in" a folder.
My friend looks as her mother, with the same smile. Which word is wrong?

My friend looks like her mother, with the same smile.
Why: "Look like" compares appearance with a noun; "as" would need a whole clause after it.
My little sister is not anymore a baby. Is the word order right?

My little sister is not a baby anymore.
Why: "Anymore" normally goes at the end of the sentence.
My manager mentioned me about the new project yesterday. What is wrong?

My manager mentioned the new project to me yesterday.
Why: "Mention" takes the thing mentioned directly, and the person comes after "to".
The Earth is round, but from the ground it looks like flat. What should I change?

The Earth is round, but from the ground it looks flat.
Why: "Look" is followed directly by an adjective; "look like" needs a noun.
Water covers most of the Earth surface. Is something missing?

Water covers most of the Earth's surface.
Why: The possessive needs an apostrophe and "s": "the Earth's surface".
